posts.title: MCP Sampling: Letting a Server Borrow the Client's Model
posts.subtitle: Nested LLM calls, with a human still in the loop
posts.summary: Sampling is the MCP primitive that lets a server ask the client to run a model completion on its behalf via sampling/createMessage, instead of the server needing its own API key. It's designed for agentic servers that need a nested reasoning step, and the spec explicitly wants a human able to review both the outgoing prompt and the incoming response.

slides.title: The server that needs to think, without its own model
slides.body: MCP servers expose tools, resources, and prompts — but what if the server itself needs an LLM to reason, summarize, or decide something mid-task? Sampling lets it ask the client to run that completion, rather than bundling its own API key and model choice.

slides.title: Without it: every agentic server needs its own model
slides.body: A search server that wants to triage ten scraped pages down to the three relevant ones needs some model to do that triage. Without sampling, it either bundles its own API key and config (cost, provider lock-in, duplicated setup for every server) or dumps all ten raw pages into the calling agent's context and makes the orchestrator do the filtering.
bullets: Bundling a model per server means N servers = N separate API bills and configs
Pushing raw data into the orchestrator's context bloats it with things the top-level agent never needed to see
Neither option lets the user's client control which model is actually doing the work

slides.title: sampling/createMessage: a request, not a bundled API key
slides.body: The server sends a sampling/createMessage request with the conversation so far, an optional system prompt, a maxTokens limit, and modelPreferences. The client — which already has a model connection — runs the completion and returns an assistant message with role, content, the model actually used, and a stop reason.
bullets: modelPreferences carries costPriority, speedPriority, and intelligencePriority as normalized 0-1 hints
Model hints are substring-based suggestions ('prefer something like claude-haiku') — advisory only, not a hard requirement
The client makes the final model choice; hints just steer it

slides.title: The spec's core requirement: a human SHOULD be in the loop
slides.body: Sampling inverts MCP's usual direction — server asks client, not client asks server — which is exactly why the spec leans hard on human oversight. Clients are expected to let users review and edit the outgoing prompt, and review the response, before either one is finalized.
bullets: Applications SHOULD show clear UI for reviewing sampling requests
Users should be able to edit the prompt before it's sent, and see the response before it's returned to the server
Security guidance also covers content validation, respecting model hints, and rate limiting on the client side

slides.title: Worked example: a research server triaging results
slides.body: A web-research MCP server crawls ten pages for a query. Instead of forwarding all ten into the orchestrating agent's context, it calls sampling/createMessage with just the ten summaries and a focused prompt: 'which three are most relevant to X?' It sets costPriority high and intelligencePriority low, since triage doesn't need the strongest model.
bullets: The client (e.g. a desktop MCP host) can show the user this sub-request before running it
A fast, cheap model handles the triage; only the three chosen pages ever reach the orchestrator's context
The server never needed its own API key — it borrowed the client's model connection for one nested call

slides.title: Sampling vs. tools vs. elicitation
slides.body: All three are MCP capabilities the client must declare support for, but they move information in different directions for different reasons.

rows: Server asks client for a completion
Server asks client for human input
SHOULD be reviewable by a human

slides.title: Where sampling doesn't fit
slides.body: Sampling is not free, and it's not for everything a server does.
bullets: Many MCP clients haven't implemented sampling yet — it requires wiring up model access and review UI, so servers must treat it as optional and degrade gracefully
A human-reviewable request per call doesn't scale to tight, high-frequency loops — it's for occasional, meaningful reasoning steps, not per-token decisions
Model hints are advisory: don't write server logic that assumes a specific model actually ran

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Sampling lets servers get LLM reasoning without owning a model connection — at the cost of needing client support and, by design, a human who can see what's being asked and answered.
bullets: sampling/createMessage flips MCP's usual direction: the server requests, the client fulfills
modelPreferences are hints (cost/speed/intelligence priorities), not guarantees — the client picks the actual model
The spec wants a human able to review both the outgoing prompt and the returned completion
Treat it as optional: not every client supports it, so servers need a fallback path

questions.prompt: What JSON-RPC method does a server call to request a model completion from the client?
options: tools/call
resources/read
sampling/createMessage
elicitation/create
questions.explanation: sampling/createMessage is the method a server sends when it wants the client to run an LLM completion on its behalf, passing messages, an optional system prompt, maxTokens, and modelPreferences.

questions.prompt: What does the MCP spec say about human involvement in sampling requests?
options: Humans should never see sampling requests, to keep latency low
A human SHOULD be able to review and edit the prompt and review the response before either is finalized
Only server administrators may approve sampling requests
Human review is required only for requests over a certain token count
questions.explanation: Because sampling lets a server trigger model usage through the client, the spec expects the client to give users a way to see and edit the outgoing prompt and to review the response before it goes back to the server.

questions.prompt: What are modelPreferences (costPriority, speedPriority, intelligencePriority) in a sampling request?
options: Hard requirements the client must obey exactly
Billing tiers the user is charged
Advisory hints — the client makes the final model choice
A list of banned models
questions.explanation: modelPreferences and model hints are advisory: they steer the client toward a cheaper, faster, or more capable model, but the client always makes the final selection — servers shouldn't assume a specific model ran.

posts.title: FreeToken: Running 700B+ MoE Models on a Gaming PC
posts.subtitle: Datacenter-scale weights, one consumer GPU
posts.summary: FreeToken is an open-source inference engine that runs frontier-scale Mixture-of-Experts models — up to 753B parameters — on a single consumer GPU by treating PCIe bandwidth and host RAM as first-class resources instead of assuming a datacenter cluster. It does this with bandwidth-adaptive CPU-GPU co-execution, an LRU cache for expert weights, and streaming prefill, and ships as real, MIT/Apache-licensed code supporting 20+ open MoE models.

slides.title: A 753B-parameter model, one workstation GPU
slides.body: FreeToken (arXiv 2608.16157, 'Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution') is an open-source engine that runs frontier-scale open-weight MoE models locally — no cluster, no datacenter NVLink, just a single GPU and a lot of clever memory management.

slides.title: MoE models are huge, but only sparsely awake
slides.body: A model like GLM-5.2 has 744B total parameters but activates roughly 40B of them per token. The problem: even though most of the model sits idle for any given token, every parameter still has to live somewhere — and 'somewhere' has traditionally meant many datacenter GPUs with high-bandwidth interconnects.
bullets: Consumer GPUs top out around 24GB VRAM — nowhere near enough for a 284B-753B parameter model
Naive CPU offload is bottlenecked by PCIe, which is an order of magnitude slower than GPU-to-GPU NVLink
Most local-inference tooling assumes the whole model fits on the device it runs on

slides.title: Treat cold experts as a caching problem, not a loading problem
slides.body: FreeToken keeps 'hot' experts resident in GPU VRAM and streams 'cold' ones from host RAM over PCIe on demand, overlapping that transfer with compute instead of stalling on it.
bullets: Bandwidth-adaptive CPU-GPU co-execution splits token routing between VRAM-resident and RAM-resident experts based on live PCIe throughput
A global LRU cache keeps frequently-activated experts on the GPU and evicts cold ones automatically
Double-buffered prefill streams the next layer's weights in while the current layer is still computing
Dynamic VRAM reallocation moves memory between the expert cache and the KV cache without restarting the engine

slides.title: Semantic caching cuts the agentic tax too
slides.body: Long agent loops re-send overlapping context on every turn. FreeToken adds semantic-aware caching for KV states across recurring context, so a multi-turn coding-agent session doesn't pay full prefill cost on every round trip — on top of quantized formats (MXFP4, NVFP4, FP8, BF16) that shrink the weights it has to move in the first place.
bullets: Built on lessons from mini-sglang, extended for consumer hardware constraints
Supports 20+ open MoE families: DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.3-Flash/5.2/4.7, Qwen3.8/3.6 MoE and dense, gpt-oss, Gemma-4, MiniMax-M2.5, and more
Apache 2.0 licensed, with a CLI and desktop app for local serving

slides.title: What hardware tier gets you which model size
slides.body: The paper's headline numbers are about scale-per-device, not raw tokens/sec — the achievement is making these sizes runnable locally at all.

rows: Largest model demonstrated in the paper

slides.title: Worked example: serving Qwen3.6-35B-A3B locally
slides.body: The '-A3B' suffix is Qwen's own naming convention for its MoE line: 35B total parameters, but only about 3B active per token. Point FreeToken's CLI at the checkpoint and it starts a local HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:1919 that accepts standard chat-completion requests — the routing between resident and streamed experts happens transparently underneath.
bullets: Because only ~3B params are active per token, most of the 35B never has to leave host RAM for a given request
The engine decides per-token which experts are worth keeping hot based on recent activation history
From the caller's side, it looks like any other local OpenAI-compatible endpoint

slides.title: The tradeoffs that don't disappear
slides.body: Bandwidth adaptation narrows the gap to datacenter serving — it doesn't close it. Some models carry real memory taxes even with the optimizations.
bullets: PCIe is still the ceiling: single-user interactive latency, not high-throughput multi-user serving
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next alone pins a 47.7 GiB n-gram table in host RAM — some models have model-specific costs beyond raw parameter count
The README is explicit that only certain checkpoints are 'known-good' — kernels are tuned for specific architectures, and other checkpoints of the same family may run but aren't guaranteed

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: FreeToken's contribution isn't a new model — it's proof that the assumption 'frontier MoE needs a datacenter' is a serving-engine limitation, not a fundamental one.
bullets: MoE sparsity means most parameters are cold for any given token — that's a caching problem, and caching problems have caching solutions
Bandwidth-adaptive CPU-GPU co-execution + an LRU expert cache lets a 753B model run on one workstation GPU
It's best suited to single-user, interactive local use — not a drop-in replacement for datacenter-scale multi-tenant serving
Real, open code (Apache 2.0, 20+ supported models) — not just a paper result

questions.prompt: Why can a 753B-parameter MoE model run on a single consumer GPU at all?
options: The model is fully quantized to 1-bit precision
Only a small fraction of experts activate per token, so most parameters can stay off-GPU until needed
FreeToken deletes unused experts permanently
Consumer GPUs now have as much VRAM as datacenter GPUs
questions.explanation: MoE sparsity means a token only routes through a handful of experts. FreeToken exploits that by keeping hot experts in VRAM and streaming cold ones from host RAM on demand, instead of requiring the entire model resident at once.

questions.prompt: What is the main bottleneck FreeToken is designed around?
options: GPU compute (FLOPs)
Model accuracy loss from quantization
PCIe bandwidth between host RAM and the GPU
Network latency to a remote API
questions.explanation: Once experts have to be streamed from CPU RAM instead of sitting in VRAM, PCIe bandwidth — far slower than GPU-to-GPU NVLink in datacenters — becomes the limiting factor. FreeToken's bandwidth-adaptive execution and double-buffered streaming exist specifically to hide that latency.

questions.prompt: What kind of workload is FreeToken best suited for, according to its own tradeoffs?
options: High-throughput serving for thousands of concurrent users
Single-user, interactive local inference
Training new models from scratch
Replacing datacenter clusters for enterprise API serving
questions.explanation: Because it's still bounded by PCIe bandwidth rather than NVLink, FreeToken trades multi-tenant throughput for the ability to run a huge model locally for one user — a fundamentally different use case than datacenter serving.

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Making Models Think Longer, Not Bigger
posts.subtitle: Why spending more compute at answer-time — not just training-time — is now how top models get smarter.
posts.summary: Test-time compute scaling spends extra inference compute — through parallel sampling, verifier-guided search, or longer reasoning chains — to boost accuracy on hard problems without retraining. It amplifies a model's existing skill but pays off only when a problem is checkable and the base model already has partial competence.

slides.title: The New Scaling Axis: Inference, Not Just Parameters
slides.body: For years, 'scale' meant bigger models and more training data. Test-time compute scaling adds a third axis: spend more compute while answering a single question.

slides.title: Bigger Models Alone Hit Diminishing Returns on Hard Reasoning
bullets: Training-time scaling (more parameters, more data) keeps costing more for smaller accuracy gains on multi-step reasoning like competition math or complex coding.
A single greedy forward pass commits to one reasoning path — if the model takes a wrong turn early, nothing catches or corrects it before the final answer.
Many hard problems are 'verifiable' — a final answer or an intermediate step can be checked — but a plain one-shot generation never uses that check at all.

slides.title: Three Ways to Spend Extra Compute at Answer Time
slides.body: Same weights, same model — the difference is how much structured compute goes into producing one answer.
bullets: Parallel sampling: generate N independent answers, then pick the most common one (self-consistency / majority vote) or the one a verifier scores highest (best-of-N).
Sequential compute: let the model produce a much longer internal reasoning trace before committing to an answer — the approach behind modern reasoning models like OpenAI's o-series and DeepSeek-R1.
Guided search: use a process reward model to score partial reasoning steps and expand only the promising branches — conceptually similar to how AlphaGo's value network pruned its game-tree search.
Sampling and search need no retraining of the base model; sequential reasoning models are specifically trained (often with RL on verifiable rewards) to make good use of extra thinking tokens.

slides.title: One Math Problem, Three Ways to Spend the Budget
slides.body: Take a competition-style word problem the base model only solves correctly on 4 out of 10 tries.
bullets: Single sample: ask once, accept whatever comes out — roughly 40% correct, no better than the model's raw skill.

Self-consistency, N=32: sample 32 independent solutions and take the majority final answer — wrong paths tend to disagree with each other on the wrong answer while correct paths converge on the same one, pushing accuracy well above any single sample.

Verifier-guided search: at each reasoning step, branch into a few candidate next steps and keep only the ones a step-level verifier still rates as on-track, pruning weak branches before they run to completion.
Nothing about the model changed — only the compute strategy wrapped around it did.

slides.title: Sampling vs. Search vs. Longer Chains

rows: N× the forward passes, no training needed
Clean final answers you can vote on (math, multiple-choice)
N× passes plus a trained reward/verifier model
Long multi-step tasks where partial correctness is checkable
Many more output tokens per single answer
Open-ended reasoning with no easy way to sample-and-vote

slides.title: Where Test-Time Compute Stops Paying Off
bullets: Returns diminish fast: going from 1 to 8 samples helps a lot; going from 32 to 256 on the same problem rarely moves accuracy much further.
It amplifies existing skill, it doesn't add missing knowledge — if the base model has no real grasp of the domain, more samples or longer chains just produce more confidently wrong answers.
Latency and cost scale directly with the compute spent, so a real-time chatbot can't afford the budget a batch research job can.
Skip it for simple, low-stakes queries — a definition lookup or a short factual question — where a single fast pass is already reliable and the extra spend buys nothing.

slides.title: Why This Reshaped How Labs Build Reasoning Models
bullets: Model quality is no longer just a training-time story — how a model is allowed to spend inference compute is now a first-class design choice.
Modern 'reasoning models' bake extended sequential compute directly into the model via reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards, instead of relying only on bolt-on sampling tricks.
The practical skill for builders shifted from just 'write a better prompt' to 'choose the right compute-spending strategy for this task's shape and budget.'

questions.prompt: What does self-consistency (majority voting) actually do?
options: Reduces the model's parameter count
Picks the most common final answer across several independently sampled solutions
Trains a new verifier model from scratch
Compresses the context window into fewer tokens
questions.explanation: Self-consistency samples multiple independent reasoning paths for the same question and takes the answer most paths agree on — wrong paths tend to diverge from each other while correct paths tend to converge on the same answer.

questions.prompt: Why is verifier-guided search compared to AlphaGo's approach?
options: It relies only on human feedback labels
It compresses model weights before inference
It scores partial progress and prunes weak branches instead of completing every possible path
It requires no additional inference compute
questions.explanation: Like a value network pruning a game tree in AlphaGo, a process reward model scores partial reasoning steps so the search can drop weak branches early instead of wasting compute finishing every possible path.

questions.prompt: When does extra test-time compute provide the LEAST benefit?
options: On hard multi-step problems the model can partially solve
On problems the base model has no relevant knowledge or skill for at all
On tasks with a clean, checkable final answer
When a verifier can reliably score partial progress
questions.explanation: Test-time compute amplifies a model's existing skill — sampling more or reasoning longer can't inject knowledge or ability the base model never had; it just produces more confident wrong answers.

posts.title: Terminal-Universe: Trajectories Become Training Environments
posts.subtitle: One Alibaba paper turns 37,300 recycled agent runs into fresh terminal-coding gyms.
posts.summary: Terminal-Universe (Qwen Team, Alibaba) reconstructs runnable coding environments by replaying the file operations already recorded in agent trajectories, then synthesizes new multi-round tasks inside them. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B on the resulting 37.3k environments lifted Terminal-Bench 2.1 by 11.9 points and EvoCode-Bench v2 multi-round by 13.8 points.

slides.title: Every Agent Trajectory Is a Buried Environment
slides.body: Alibaba's Qwen team found a way to resurrect the exact workspace an agent worked in — and turn it into a brand-new coding task.

slides.title: Terminal Agents Have Logs but Nowhere to Train
bullets: Millions of terminal-agent trajectories exist online — but the actual repos and file systems they ran in are gone or private.
Hand-building realistic multi-file coding environments (Docker images, dependencies, seed bugs) doesn't scale past a few thousand tasks.
Without fresh environments, fine-tuning data goes stale and models overfit to the same handful of benchmark repos.

slides.title: Replay the File Ops Backward to Rebuild the Workspace
slides.body: Every trajectory already records which files the agent touched — that's enough to reverse-engineer the environment it started in.
bullets: Replay recorded file edits in reverse to restore the pre-agent workspace — a 'partial workspace' with gaps where files were fully overwritten.
A completion agent fills the missing files and dependencies so the reconstructed environment actually runs.
Breadth: mine dependency links between reconstructed repos to synthesize cross-workspace queries spanning multiple codebases.
Depth: a 'user agent' extends a single-turn ask into a multi-round session with iterative feedback and requirement changes.

slides.title: From One Bug Fix to a Fresh Multi-File Task
slides.body: A concrete walkthrough of the pipeline on a single trajectory.
bullets: Source trajectory: an agent patched a null-pointer bug across 3 files in a Python service.
Terminal-Universe reverses the diff, restoring those 3 files, and flags any it can't fully recover.
A completion agent regenerates the missing files and imports so the repo builds again.
A new task is synthesized in that same repo — e.g. 'add input validation to the same endpoint' — a task nobody wrote by hand.

slides.title: The Payoff: 37.3K Environments, Real Benchmark Gains
bullets: Applied to public trajectories, the pipeline produced 37,300 task-sufficient environments — far beyond what hand-curation could reach.

slides.title: Where This Breaks Down
bullets: Reconstructed environments are approximations, not ground truth — the completion agent can silently paper over files it can't fully recover.
Quality is capped by the diversity of the source trajectories — mining from a narrow trajectory pool just recycles the same patterns.
Running a completion agent plus a user agent for every trajectory adds real compute cost before a single training example exists.
Skip this if you already have a curated, verified environment suite — reconstruction is for scaling coverage, not replacing hand-checked benchmarks.

slides.title: Why This Matters for Agent Training
bullets: Training data for terminal/coding agents has been the bottleneck, not model architecture — this attacks that bottleneck directly.
The 'reconstruct-from-logs' trick generalizes beyond terminal agents to any domain where trajectories imply an environment.
Expect more labs to mine their own agent logs this way instead of paying for hand-built environments.

The recorded file operations in the agent's trajectory
A human-written environment spec
The model's training data
questions.explanation: The trajectory's tool-execution history reveals which files existed and how they changed, which is enough to rebuild the workspace the agent originally ran in.

options: The original human developer

Manual annotation
questions.explanation: A completion agent generates the missing files and dependencies so the reconstructed 'partial workspace' becomes a runnable environment again.

+11.9 points
+37 points
+71 points
questions.explanation: The paper reports an 11.9-point single-round gain on Terminal-Bench 2.1, plus a 13.8-point multi-round gain on EvoCode-Bench v2.

posts.title: ReAct: The Loop Behind Every Modern AI Agent
posts.subtitle: Think, act, observe, repeat — the simple pattern that made LLM agents work.
posts.summary: ReAct interleaves short reasoning traces with tool calls and their real outputs, so each new thought is grounded in an actual observation instead of a guess. It's the pattern underneath nearly every modern tool-using agent, and it needed almost no extra training to work.

slides.title: Why Can Agents Use Tools at All?
slides.body: One 2022 idea — interleave reasoning with action — is still the backbone of nearly every tool-using LLM agent today.

slides.title: Reasoning Alone Can't Touch the Real World
bullets: Chain-of-thought makes a model think step by step — but it's still just talking to itself, with no way to check a fact or take an action.
Acting alone (calling tools with no visible reasoning) works but gives no way to tell why the model chose an action, or to catch it going wrong.
Real tasks need both: decide what to do, do it, see what happened, and adjust.

slides.title: Interleave Thought, Action, and Observation
slides.body: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) has the model alternate three steps in one running transcript.
bullets: Thought: a short reasoning trace — 'I need the current weather to answer this.'
Action: a tool call — search("weather in Paris").
Observation: the tool's real output gets appended back into the context.
The loop repeats — each new thought is grounded in a real observation, not a guess.

slides.title: Worked Example: Multi-Hop Question Answering
slides.body: Question: which magazine was started first, Arthur's Magazine or First for Women?
bullets: Thought 1: 'I need Arthur's Magazine's launch date.' Action: search("Arthur's Magazine"). Observation: '1844'.
Thought 2: 'Now I need First for Women's launch date.' Action: search("First for Women"). Observation: '1989'.
Thought 3: '1844 predates 1989.' Action: finish("Arthur's Magazine").
Each hop is checked against a real search result instead of the model guessing both dates from memory.

slides.title: The Numbers That Made It Stick
bullets: On ALFWorld, ReAct beat imitation-learning and RL baselines trained on thousands of examples — using just 1-2 in-context examples.

slides.title: When the Loop Breaks Down
bullets: Error compounding: a wrong observation early on (a bad search result, a flaky tool) drags every later thought off course.
Cost: every thought and observation goes back into the context, so long-horizon tasks burn tokens fast.
Latency: each tool call is a round trip — not the right pattern for a task that needs one instant answer with no lookup.
Skip it for pure knowledge-recall tasks where the model already knows the answer cold — the extra tool calls just add latency for no gain.

slides.title: Why This Pattern Won
bullets: ReAct is the ancestor of nearly every agent framework's loop — LangChain agents, AutoGPT-style runners, and most 'tool-calling' LLM APIs use this exact think-act-observe structure.
The core insight: reasoning grounded in real tool feedback beats reasoning alone or acting alone.
It needs almost no extra training — 1-2 examples in the prompt is enough, which is why it spread so fast.

questions.prompt: What are the three steps ReAct interleaves in a single loop?
options: Plan, Execute, Report
Thought, Action, Observation
Encode, Decode, Rank
Search, Rank, Answer
questions.explanation: ReAct alternates a reasoning trace (Thought), a tool call (Action), and the tool's real result (Observation), feeding each observation back into the next thought.

questions.prompt: On ALFWorld, how did ReAct compare to BUTLER, an imitation-learning baseline trained on thousands of examples?
options: ReAct scored lower using far less training data
ReAct matched it exactly
ReAct beat it by 34 points using only 1-2 in-context examples
They weren't compared on the same benchmark
questions.explanation: ReAct reached 71% success versus BUTLER's 37% — a 34-point gap — despite using only one or two in-context examples instead of thousands of training trajectories.

questions.prompt: What's a key failure mode of the ReAct loop?
options: It cannot call external tools
A bad early observation can compound and derail every later reasoning step
It only works with reasoning models
It requires no context window
questions.explanation: Because each new thought is conditioned on the previous observation, one bad tool result (a flaky search, a stale API) can send the rest of the trajectory off track.

posts.title: Atlas: World Labs' Omni Model for Spatial Intelligence
posts.subtitle: One rectified-flow transformer turns a single photo into a minute of pixel-perfect, camera-controlled 3D world.
posts.summary: World Labs (Fei-Fei Li's startup) launched Atlas, an omni world model that natively handles text, image, video, and 3D in one autoregressive diffusion transformer, generating 1440p camera-controlled video up to a minute long from a single image. It builds on Marble's spatial representation, but shipped without a paper, model card, or pricing.

slides.title: A model that thinks in 3D, not just pixels
slides.body: On September 1, 2026, World Labs unveiled Atlas: a single model pretrained from scratch to operate natively across text, images, video, and 3D — not four separate models bolted together.
bullets: Built by World Labs, the spatial-intelligence startup co-founded by Fei-Fei Li
Generates images and video from one or more input images with precise camera control
Outputs up to 1 minute of video at 1440p resolution

slides.title: Video generators don't know they're in a place
slides.body: Most generative video models predict plausible next frames but have no persistent notion of 3D space — move the camera and the room quietly reconfigures itself.
bullets: Image, video, and 3D generation have historically needed separate specialized models
Standard video diffusion has no explicit 3D state, so consistency degrades over longer camera moves
Robotics and simulation need geometry that stays consistent, not just visually plausible frames

slides.title: One shared spatial context, one transformer
slides.body: Atlas is a multimodal autoregressive diffusion transformer — specifically a rectified-flow model — where text, image, video, and 3D inputs are fused into a single spatial context the model extends.
bullets: All modalities are combined into shared context; the model predicts what comes next while staying geometrically consistent with everything already generated
Pretrained from scratch (not fine-tuned from a video model) so 3D consistency is a first-class training objective, not an afterthought
Shares its core spatial representation with Marble, World Labs' earlier commercial model (launched Nov 2025, now at v1.1)
Atlas is positioned to power future versions of Marble and other World Labs products

slides.title: Human raters preferred Atlas across the board
slides.body: World Labs ran blind camera-controlled generation comparisons with third-party human raters against five other systems.

slides.title: One photo becomes a walkable set
slides.body: Feed Atlas a single photo of a room, and it can extrapolate a full 3D environment beyond the frame: pan the camera left and it renders wall and furniture that were never in the source image, staying consistent if you pan back.
bullets: Concrete use case: a game studio drops in one concept-art still and gets a navigable 1-minute flythrough at 1440p to previz a level
Robotics use case: generate synthetic robot-eye-view footage of a scene from novel camera angles for training data, without a physical camera rig

slides.title: Impressive demo, unverifiable claims
slides.body: The launch shipped with no technical paper, no model card, no public pricing, and no named launch partner — every benchmark number above comes from World Labs' own evaluation, run by World Labs.
bullets: No independent reproduction of the rater study exists yet — treat the 75-94% preference numbers as a vendor claim, not a peer-reviewed result
Without a model card, compute cost, context limits, and failure modes (e.g. very long camera paths, cluttered scenes) are unknown
Access details (API, waitlist, cost) were not disclosed at launch, so it isn't yet usable in most production pipelines

slides.title: Watch the category, not just the model
bullets: Atlas argues that 3D/video/image generation converge into one omni model rather than staying separate specialties
The rectified-flow, shared-spatial-context design is the real idea — Atlas is one implementation of it
Until an independent paper or benchmark appears, read the preference numbers as a strong marketing claim from a well-funded lab, not settled science

posts.title: LatentPress: Compressing Context Into Memory Tokens
posts.subtitle: 7.7x smaller than raw context and more accurate than either — because a text summary throws away exactly what a model needs.
posts.summary: LatentPress compresses long conversational or document context into a short sequence of continuous memory tokens that a frozen decoder reads directly, instead of collapsing it into a human-readable text summary. On LongMemEval it beats both raw uncompressed context and text-summary baselines while using 7.7x less context.

slides.title: Compress the context, not just the words
slides.body: LatentPress, a new paper trending on Hugging Face's Daily Papers, compresses long context into continuous 'memory tokens' a model reads directly — skipping the lossy step of turning it back into English first.
bullets: Targets long conversational and document context, the same problem RAG and prompt caching also attack
Reports 0.504 accuracy at 7.70x compression on LongMemEval, versus 0.490 for uncompressed evidence
Trains only a small adapter (4.2M-26.2M params) while keeping the base decoder frozen

slides.title: Every existing shortcut leaks information
slides.body: Long context is expensive to keep around and slow to replay every turn, but the obvious fixes for shrinking it both destroy exactly the details a later query might need.
bullets: Text summarization is lossy by construction — LatentPress reports summaries scoring only 0.184 accuracy on LongMemEval, far below raw context
OCR-based / textual compression degrades further as you push the compression ratio harder (0.426 down to 0.312 in the paper's tests)
Keeping the full raw transcript avoids the accuracy loss but keeps the latency and memory cost of a long context window

slides.title: A small writer, a frozen reader
slides.body: Instead of compressing text into shorter text, LatentPress trains a compact 'writer' model to compress context directly into continuous memory tokens that the existing decoder can read, with no fine-tuning of the decoder itself.
bullets: The writer is reader-matched: built to produce tokens the target decoder already understands, so only a lightweight adapter needs training
Adapter size: 4.2M-26.2M parameters — a small fraction of the base model
Achieves 4-16x compression depending on configuration, with the 7.7x setting as the reported sweet spot
Because the output is dense memory tokens rather than replayed text, writing is fast (~43ms per conversation) and reading back is 5-9x faster than processing raw context

slides.title: Compression that doesn't cost accuracy
slides.body: On LongMemEval, LatentPress is the only compression method that matches or beats the uncompressed baseline.

slides.title: A support agent that remembers 50 turns without replaying them
slides.body: Picture a customer-support agent mid-conversation with 50 turns of history: the order number, three prior troubleshooting attempts, and a refund policy exception mentioned in turn 12.
bullets: Replaying all 50 turns as raw text keeps every detail but costs latency and context budget on every single reply
Summarizing to text risks compressing away the exact refund exception the agent needs at turn 51
LatentPress instead compresses the 50 turns into a short run of memory tokens the decoder reads natively, preserving the fine detail while cutting the token footprint ~7.7x

slides.title: The catch: opaque, and coupled to one reader
bullets: Memory tokens are not human-readable — unlike a text summary, you can't eyeball them to debug what the model 'remembers'
The writer is reader-matched, meaning a compressor trained for one decoder doesn't necessarily transfer to a different model family
Results are reported on LongMemEval specifically; broader generalization across task types and much longer horizons isn't yet established
This is a research result, not yet a shipped inference-stack feature — expect a gap before it appears in production serving frameworks

slides.title: Compress in latent space, not in English
bullets: The core idea: what you compress into matters as much as how much you compress — continuous tokens preserve more than text ever can
7.7x smaller context with a small accuracy gain over uncompressed, not just 'good enough' — a rare free lunch in this space
Best read alongside prompt caching and KV-cache compression as another tool for the same underlying problem: context is the bottleneck for long-running agents

questions.prompt: What does LatentPress compress long context into?
options: A shorter plain-text summary
Continuous memory tokens read directly by a frozen decoder
A compressed image representation
A SQL database of extracted facts
questions.explanation: Unlike text summarization, LatentPress's writer produces continuous memory tokens tailored to the target decoder, avoiding the lossy round-trip through natural language.

questions.prompt: On LongMemEval, how did text summarization compare to LatentPress?
options: Text summarization scored higher accuracy (0.184 vs a lower LatentPress score)
They scored identically
Text summarization scored only 0.184 accuracy, far below LatentPress's 0.504
Text summarization wasn't tested in the paper
questions.explanation: The paper reports text summaries at just 0.184 accuracy, illustrating how much task-relevant detail a natural-language summary throws away compared to LatentPress's memory tokens.

questions.prompt: What is a real limitation of LatentPress noted in this post?
options: It requires no training at all, so results can't be trusted
The memory tokens aren't human-readable and the writer is matched to one specific reader model, limiting portability
It only works on images, not text
It is slower than replaying raw context in every case
questions.explanation: Because the writer is reader-matched and its output is opaque memory tokens, you lose the debuggability of a text summary and can't freely swap in a different decoder without retraining the adapter.

posts.title: RoPE: Encoding Position by Rotating Embeddings
posts.subtitle: Why rotating query and key vectors gives a transformer relative position for free — no extra parameters, no added tokens.
posts.summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) injects position by rotating each query/key vector by an angle proportional to its token position, so the attention dot product between any two positions depends only on their relative distance. It's the positional scheme behind LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, and most modern open LLMs — but it needs extra tricks to extend past its trained context length.

slides.title: Self-attention has no sense of order
slides.body: Swap two tokens in a sequence and vanilla self-attention produces the same output for the rest — it treats input as a bag, not a sequence. Something has to inject position, and RoPE does it by rotation.
bullets: Introduced in the 2021 RoFormer paper (Su et al.) and now used in LLaMA, GPT-NeoX, PaLM, Qwen, and Mistral
Adds zero extra parameters and no extra tokens — position is applied as a transformation at attention time

slides.title: Absolute position embeddings don't encode distance
slides.body: The original Transformer and BERT add a position vector to each token's embedding — the model has to learn from data that position 5 and position 6 are 'close', and that lesson often breaks past the lengths seen in training.
bullets: Learned absolute embeddings (BERT-style) simply have no vector for a position they never saw during training — they can't extrapolate at all
Sinusoidal absolute embeddings (original Transformer) extrapolate somewhat but still encode position additively, not as a direct function of relative distance
What attention actually needs is 'how far apart are these two tokens', not 'where is each token in isolation'

slides.title: Rotate each vector by an angle proportional to position
slides.body: RoPE splits each query/key vector into 2D pairs of dimensions and rotates every pair by an angle m·θ, where m is the token's position and θ is a frequency specific to that dimension pair.
bullets: Different dimension pairs use different frequencies (like Fourier features): low-frequency pairs track long-range position, high-frequency pairs track fine-grained local position
The rotation is applied to Q and K right before the attention dot product — V is untouched
Key identity: rotating Q by angle m·θ and K by angle n·θ makes their dot product depend only on (m-n) — the relative offset — not on m or n individually
Original RoFormer uses base frequency θ_base = 10000, the same base later reused (and re-tuned) by most LLaMA-family models

slides.title: Same rotation gap, same attention score
slides.body: Take a simplified 2D case with a fixed frequency θ. Rotating Q at position 5 and K at position 8 leaves a relative angle of 3θ between them. Shift both tokens 100 positions later — Q at 105, K at 108 — and the relative angle is still 3θ.
bullets: The dot product between the rotated vectors is identical in both cases, because only the relative gap (3 positions) entered the rotation math
This is what 'relative position for free' means: the model never needs to have seen position 108 specifically — only the offset of 3 needs to generalize
Contrast with an absolute embedding table: a vector for position 108 either exists in the learned table or it doesn't

slides.title: Where RoPE sits among positional schemes

rows: No — no vector exists past max length
Degrades gracefully, needs scaling tricks past trained length

slides.title: RoPE still breaks past its trained length
slides.body: The relative-position trick doesn't make RoPE infinitely extensible: push far enough past the training context length and the low-frequency rotations effectively 'wrap around', and quality degrades.
bullets: Naively running a RoPE model at 4x its trained context length typically produces incoherent output well before hitting the wall

Fixes are extensions to RoPE itself, not replacements: Position Interpolation compresses positions to fit the trained range; NTK-aware scaling and YaRN reweight frequencies non-uniformly to preserve local precision while stretching long-range reach
This is why context-length upgrades in LLaMA-family models are usually announced together with a specific RoPE-scaling method, not just 'we trained on longer sequences'

slides.title: Rotation, not addition, is the key idea
bullets: RoPE encodes position by rotating Q/K at attention time, so the attention score naturally depends only on relative distance
Zero added parameters, zero added tokens — the mechanism is a fixed rotation applied per dimension-pair, per position
It doesn't extrapolate for free past training length — expect any long-context model built on RoPE to pair it with an explicit scaling method like YaRN

questions.prompt: What does RoPE actually do to query and key vectors?
options: Adds a learned position vector to the token embedding before the first layer
Rotates pairs of dimensions in Q and K by an angle proportional to token position, applied at attention time
Concatenates a one-hot position vector to each token
Inserts special position tokens into the input sequence
questions.explanation: RoPE treats each pair of dimensions as a 2D plane and rotates it by m·θ, where m is the position and θ is a per-pair frequency — applied to Q and K right before the attention dot product, not added to the input embedding.

questions.prompt: Why does rotating Q and K give attention a 'relative position' property?
options: Because rotation matrices are always symmetric
Because the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the difference between their rotation angles, i.e. the relative token offset
Because rotation removes position information entirely, forcing the model to ignore order
Because rotating vectors always increases their magnitude proportionally to position
questions.explanation: The rotation identity means the dot product between Q at position m and K at position n only depends on (m−n), so the same relative offset produces the same attention contribution no matter where it occurs in the sequence.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of RoPE this post highlights?
options: It requires far more parameters than absolute position embeddings
It cannot be used with causal (autoregressive) attention
It degrades past the trained context length and needs scaling methods like Position Interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, or YaRN to extend safely
It only works for vision transformers, not language models
questions.explanation: RoPE's relative-position trick doesn't grant free extrapolation — going well past the trained context length causes quality to degrade, which is why long-context releases pair RoPE with an explicit frequency-rescaling method.

posts.title: Context Engineering: What Goes Into the Context Window
posts.subtitle: The context window is scarce working memory — curate it, don't just fill it.
posts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding exactly what goes into an LLM's limited context window — system instructions, tools, retrieved knowledge, and history — instead of just writing better prompts. Get it wrong and agents drift, stall, or blow through their token budget; get it right and the same model performs dramatically better.

slides.title: Prompting Got You Started. Context Engineering Keeps You Working.
slides.body: Every token in the context window competes for the model's attention and your budget. As agents grew multi-step and tool-heavy, the bottleneck moved from 'what do I ask' to 'what does the model actually see at this step.'

slides.title: A Full Context Window Isn't a Smart One
slides.body: Long-context models can technically hold hundreds of thousands of tokens, but stuffing everything in doesn't help — models systematically under-use content buried in the middle of a long context, a pattern often called 'lost in the middle.'
bullets: More tokens = more cost and latency, not automatically more accuracy
Irrelevant tool outputs and stale messages dilute the signal near the actual question
Agents that append every tool result forever eventually drown their own instructions

slides.title: Prompt Engineering Writes Words. Context Engineering Curates State.
slides.body: Prompt engineering optimizes a single instruction. Context engineering is the ongoing job of deciding what subset of available information belongs in the window for THIS step of a multi-turn task.
bullets: System prompt: stable rules and persona — changes rarely
Tool definitions: only the tools relevant to the current step, not the whole toolbox
Retrieved knowledge: RAG chunks, docs, prior outputs — filtered and ranked
Working memory: a running summary, not the full raw transcript

slides.title: The Context Window Has a Shape, Not Just a Size
slides.body: Ordering matters as much as content. Production agents typically assemble context in layers, each with its own eviction policy.
bullets: Layer 1 — system/instructions: fixed, always present, highest priority
Layer 2 — tools schema: pruned to what's callable right now, not the entire registry
Layer 3 — retrieved context: reranked, deduplicated, capped by a token budget
Layer 4 — conversation history: recent turns verbatim, older turns compacted or summarized

slides.title: A Coding Agent Runs Out of Room at Turn 40
slides.body: Concrete scenario: an autonomous coding agent debugging a failing test loop keeps appending every file read and failed command to its context. By turn 40 it's carrying tens of thousands of tokens of scrollback, most of it stale diffs and dead ends.
bullets: Fix: after each tool call, keep the result only if it's still relevant; summarize and discard the rest
Fix: replace raw diff history with a running 'state so far' summary updated each turn
Pattern used by real coding agents: a compaction pass condenses old turns into a short recap once history crosses a token threshold, freeing room for new tool output

slides.title: Context Engineering vs. Prompt Engineering vs. RAG
slides.body: These three are complementary layers, not competitors — context engineering is the umbrella that decides how the other two get used at each step.

rows: The full assembled window: instructions + tools + memory + retrieval

slides.title: Where Context Engineering Goes Wrong
slides.body: The two failure modes are opposite: too little context starves the model of what it needs; too much drowns the signal and burns budget.
bullets: Context rot: as history grows, effective attention to any single fact drops — same model, worse recall, no code change
Silent truncation: naively cutting the oldest messages can delete the original task instructions, not just old chatter
Over-retrieval: dumping the top-20 RAG chunks 'to be safe' pushes out room for reasoning and tool results
When NOT to bother: short, single-turn tasks with small fixed inputs don't need a context pipeline — plain prompting is fine

slides.title: Treat the Context Window Like Working Memory, Not a Log File
bullets: Budget tokens by layer: fixed instructions, live tools, ranked retrieval, compacted history
Summarize and evict aggressively — relevance decays, especially in the middle of long contexts
Measure it: track tokens-per-turn alongside task success, not tokens alone
Prompt engineering still matters — it's now one layer inside a larger context pipeline

questions.prompt: What does the 'lost in the middle' effect describe?
options: Models forget their system prompt after fine-tuning
Models are typically less accurate at using information placed in the middle of a long context than content near the start or end
RAG retrieval systematically skips documents ranked in the middle of a results list
Agents lose track of which tool they called two turns ago
questions.explanation: Studies of long-context models often find a U-shaped accuracy curve: strong recall for facts near the start and end of the context, weaker for content buried in the middle. Where you place critical information matters, not just whether it's included.

questions.prompt: A coding agent's context keeps filling up with old tool outputs across a long debugging session. What's the context-engineering fix?
options: Switch to a model with a larger context window and keep going
Summarize or compact stale turns and drop tool outputs that are no longer relevant, while preserving the original task instructions
Disable tool use for the rest of the session
Restart the conversation from scratch every 10 turns
questions.explanation: The fix is curation, not brute-force capacity: compact old history into a short running summary and evict content that's no longer relevant, making sure the original instructions survive any truncation.

questions.prompt: How does context engineering differ from prompt engineering?
options: They're the same practice with different marketing names
Context engineering only applies inside RAG pipelines
Prompt engineering crafts the instruction text; context engineering manages the entire assembled window — instructions, tools, memory, and retrieval — turn by turn
Context engineering removes the need for a system prompt
questions.explanation: Prompt engineering optimizes the words of a single instruction. Context engineering is the broader, ongoing job of deciding what subset of all available information, across every layer, belongs in the window at each step of a task.

posts.title: Muse Spark 1.3: Meta's Agent Learns to Ask First
posts.subtitle: Frontier coding scores, plus a model that pauses before risky changes
posts.summary: Meta shipped Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, 2026 — a frontier reasoning model for Muse Code and the Meta Model API that asks for confirmation before risky changes, reaches #6 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, and adds a steeply discounted tier for developers who let Meta train on their data.

slides.title: Meta's Agent Learns to Ask First
slides.body: Muse Spark 1.3 pairs frontier-level coding scores with a habit most agents skip: pausing to confirm before it makes a significant change.

slides.title: Confident Agents Break Things Confidently
bullets: Long-horizon coding agents that barrel through multi-step tasks without checking in can burn turns on a wrong assumption before anyone notices.
Meta's earlier Muse Spark releases lagged the coding and agentic frontier that Anthropic and OpenAI were setting.
Developers needed both higher first-attempt accuracy and a model that knows when to stop and ask, instead of one or the other.

slides.title: Higher Accuracy, With a Built-In Pause Button
slides.body: Muse Spark 1.3 tracks context and prior results across a session, works through messy or conflicting inputs, and explicitly asks for input when it needs it — including requesting confirmation before making significant changes.
bullets: Meta reports higher first-attempt accuracy and more reliable tool calling than the prior Muse Spark release.
Tuned for long-horizon coding workflows specifically: fewer unnecessary turns, cleaner output per step.

slides.title: What It Can See, and Where You Can Run It
bullets: 1M-token context window; takes text, image, and video as input, with visual reasoning run through a real execution environment instead of scripted steps.
Shipped through Muse Code (Meta's coding agent) and the Meta Model API in public preview with expanded global access — also available on OpenRouter.
Two variants: a publicly available model and a higher-scoring 'max' variant currently limited to partner preview only.

slides.title: Where It Lands on the Frontier
slides.body: On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — a composite of reasoning, knowledge, math, and coding — the publicly available variant ranks #6 of 636 tracked models; the limited-preview 'max' variant ranks #3, trailing only Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.

rows: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (max, partner preview)

slides.title: A Refactor That Stops to Check
bullets: Point Muse Code at a repo and ask for a multi-file refactor: the agent tracks what it's already changed across the session instead of re-deriving state each turn.
When it hits an ambiguous case — say, a config change that would affect a production migration path — it asks for confirmation instead of guessing and moving on.
That single pause can be the difference between one wrong turn and a cascade of wrong turns built on top of it.

slides.title: The Fine Print
bullets: The best-scoring 'max' variant (Intelligence Index 62, #3 overall) isn't broadly available — it's limited to partner preview, so most developers only get the public variant scoring 61.
A new steeply discounted Contributor tier trades price for data: Meta trains on your prompts and completions in exchange for the lower rate.
Frontier-adjacent doesn't mean frontier-leading: it's competitive with Claude Fable 5.1 on coding, not ahead of it.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Muse Spark 1.3 closes most of Meta's coding-agent gap with Anthropic and OpenAI, landing top-6 on a major composite benchmark.
Asking for confirmation before risky changes is a small design choice with an outsized effect on how much damage a wrong turn can do.
The cheapest access tier isn't free of tradeoffs — check what 'discounted' costs you in data before switching.

posts.title: Constitutional AI: Training on Principles Instead of Labels
posts.subtitle: How Anthropic replaced human harm-labels with a written constitution
posts.summary: Constitutional AI trains a harmless assistant using a small written set of principles instead of human-labeled examples of harm — the model critiques and revises its own outputs, then an AI judge (not a human) supplies the preference labels that drive reinforcement learning.

slides.title: What If the Model Graded Its Own Homework?
slides.body: Constitutional AI (CAI) swaps human harm-labels for a written set of principles — the model critiques and revises itself, then an AI judge, not a person, supplies the preference data.

slides.title: RLHF Doesn't Scale to Every New Harm
bullets: Standard RLHF needs human raters to read and rank outputs for every harmful or borderline category the model might produce.
That's slow, expensive, and taxing on the people doing the labeling — especially for graphic or disturbing content.
Different raters disagree on subjective harm judgments, so label quality drifts depending on who's labeling that batch.

slides.title: Two Phases: Self-Critique, Then AI Preference Labels
slides.body: Phase 1 (SL-CAI): the model drafts a response, critiques it against a written constitution, then revises it — the revised responses become supervised fine-tuning data. Phase 2 (RL-CAI): the model generates pairs of responses, and an AI judge picks which better follows the constitution, replacing human comparisons in the reward-model step.
bullets: Phase 2 mirrors RLHF's structure exactly — preference labels train a reward model, then PPO optimizes the policy against it — the only swap is who supplies the labels.

slides.title: The Constitution Is Just a List of Principles
bullets: A short set of natural-language rules (drawn from sources like human-rights documents or platform policy) that the model is instructed to apply when critiquing itself.
Change the constitution and you change behavior — no new human-labeled dataset required.
Principles compose: a new rule can be added later without retraining the base model from scratch.

slides.title: RLHF vs. Constitutional AI

rows: AI model, guided by written principles
Scaling to a new risk category
Add or edit a principle in the constitution
Yes — for helpfulness training and red-teaming

slides.title: Self-Critiquing a Borderline Request
bullets: A user asks how to pick a lock. A first draft either refuses bluntly or gives unsafe step-by-step detail.
The self-critique step checks that draft against a principle like 'choose the response least likely to be harmful without being condescending or preachy.'
The revision explains lockpicking is a real hobby and locksmith skill, and gives a measured, contextual answer instead of a blanket refusal or a how-to for defeating a specific lock.

slides.title: Where It Can Go Wrong
bullets: The AI judge can share the base model's own blind spots or biases — there's no independent ground truth checking it.
Principles can conflict on edge cases (being maximally helpful vs. being maximally cautious), and the model has to resolve that tension on its own.
This doesn't remove humans from the loop entirely — helpfulness training and red-teaming still rely on human data and judgment.
A poorly written constitution can push a model toward over-refusing safe requests or under-refusing genuinely harmful ones.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Constitutional AI keeps RLHF's reward-model-plus-PPO structure but replaces the human comparison step with an AI judge guided by written principles.
The constitution makes model values explicit and editable, instead of implicit in thousands of individual rater decisions.
It reduces reliance on human labels for harm, but doesn't eliminate human oversight — helpfulness and red-teaming still need people.

questions.prompt: In Constitutional AI's second phase (RL-CAI), what replaces human comparison labels?
options: A random coin flip between two responses
An AI model judging responses against a written set of principles
A rule-based keyword filter
The original RLHF reward model, unchanged

posts.title: RLHF: Teaching a Model What Humans Actually Want
posts.subtitle: Turning pairwise human preferences into a training signal a policy can optimize
posts.summary: RLHF aligns a language model by training a reward model on human pairwise rankings, then optimizing the policy against it with PPO under a KL penalty. It's the pipeline behind InstructGPT and the reference point that cheaper methods like DPO and GRPO are built to replace.

slides.title: RLHF: Teaching a Model What Humans Actually Want
slides.body: Pretraining teaches a model to predict the next token on internet text. It doesn't teach the model which of two correct answers a human would actually prefer. RLHF closes that gap.

slides.title: A Model That Predicts Text Isn't a Model That Helps You
slides.body: Pretraining minimizes next-token loss on web text, so a base model is just as likely to continue a question with more questions, a wall of caveats, or a fluent-sounding lie as with the answer you actually wanted.
bullets: A raw base model completes prompts — ask it a question and it may just generate more similar-looking questions instead of answering
There's no single 'correct' next token for 'write a poem about the ocean' — quality here is a preference, not a label
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human demonstrations helps, but hand-writing enough ideal responses for every situation doesn't scale

slides.title: Three Stages: Demonstrate, Score, Optimize
slides.body: InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) formalized the now-standard pipeline: supervised fine-tuning, then a learned reward model, then reinforcement learning against that reward model.
bullets: Stage 1 — SFT: fine-tune the base model on a small set of human-written demonstrations (prompt → ideal response)
Stage 2 — Reward Model: humans rank several SFT outputs for the same prompt; train a model to score outputs the way humans ranked them
Stage 3 — RL (PPO): the SFT model generates responses, the reward model scores them, and PPO updates the policy to raise its expected reward

slides.title: The Reward Model Learns From Rankings, Not Labels
slides.body: Labelers don't rate outputs on an absolute scale — they just say which of two responses is better. The reward model is trained on that pairwise signal with a Bradley-Terry style loss.
bullets: Loss ≈ −log(sigmoid(r(chosen) − r(rejected))) — push the score of the preferred response above the rejected one
Pairwise comparisons are far more consistent between labelers than absolute 1–10 ratings, which is why RLHF is built on rankings
The reward model is usually initialized from the SFT checkpoint itself, with the final layer swapped for a single scalar output

slides.title: PPO's KL Penalty Is a Leash, Not an Afterthought
slides.body: Maximize reward with nothing holding it back and the policy drifts into text that scores well on the reward model but reads like nonsense. PPO's objective subtracts a KL-divergence penalty against the frozen SFT model to prevent that.
bullets: Objective ≈ E[reward(response)] − β · KL(policy ‖ reference SFT model)
β is tuned per run — too low and the policy reward-hacks; too high and it barely moves off the SFT model
PPO's clipped surrogate objective also caps how far any single update can move the policy in one step

slides.title: Walking Through One Prompt
slides.body: Prompt: 'Explain photosynthesis to a 10-year-old.' The SFT model samples four different responses; a labeler ranks them best to worst.
bullets: Ranked #1: a short, concrete analogy ('plants eat sunlight like you eat food') — the reward model learns to score this style highly
Ranked #4: a technically correct but jargon-heavy paragraph about chlorophyll and ATP — scores low despite being 'more complete'
During PPO, the policy is nudged toward simpler, more concrete phrasing for this kind of prompt — without ever being told the 'right' words directly

slides.title: RLHF, DPO, and GRPO Solve the Same Problem Differently
slides.body: DPO removes the reward model and the RL loop entirely by showing the RLHF objective has a closed-form solution in terms of the policy itself. GRPO keeps RL but drops the value network by normalizing reward across a group of samples per prompt.

rows: 3: policy, reference, reward — no value net
Often — sometimes replaced by a rule-based/verifiable reward

slides.title: Reward Hacking Is the Failure Mode to Design Around
slides.body: A reward model is a proxy for human preference, not preference itself — and policies are very good at finding the gap between the two.
bullets: Verbosity bias: reward models frequently favor longer answers, so unconstrained RLHF tends to make outputs bloated
Sycophancy: a reward model trained on human ratings can reward agreeable-sounding answers over correct ones

Cost: RLHF needs a labeling pipeline, a trained reward model, and up to 4 models resident in memory during training — for narrow, in-domain tasks, SFT alone or DPO is often 'good enough' and far cheaper
Alignment tax: RLHF'd models can measurably regress on certain benchmarks (e.g. calibration, some factual QA) relative to the SFT-only checkpoint

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: RLHF turns 'what humans prefer' into a trainable signal: a reward model learns from pairwise rankings, then PPO optimizes a policy against it
The KL penalty against the reference model is what keeps optimization from collapsing into reward hacking
DPO and GRPO are direct responses to RLHF's cost — DPO removes the RL loop, GRPO removes the value network
InstructGPT showed a 1.3B RLHF'd model's outputs were preferred by human labelers over the base 175B GPT-3 — parameter count alone doesn't determine helpfulness

questions.prompt: In PPO-based RLHF, what does the KL-divergence penalty term do?
options: Increases the reward for longer responses
Keeps the policy from drifting too far from the reference SFT model, limiting reward hacking
Removes the need for a reward model
Speeds up training by skipping the reference model entirely
questions.explanation: Without the KL penalty, the policy is free to over-optimize the reward model's quirks and produce fluent-looking but low-quality text. The KL term anchors it to the SFT model's distribution of reasonable text.

questions.prompt: What is the key structural difference between DPO and PPO-based RLHF?
options: DPO doesn't use human preference data at all
DPO trains a separate value network instead of a reward model
DPO eliminates the separate reward model and RL rollouts by optimizing a closed-form loss directly on the policy
DPO requires more models in memory than PPO
questions.explanation: DPO reformulates the RLHF objective algebraically so the optimal policy can be trained directly from preference pairs with a single loss — no reward model, no on-policy sampling, no PPO clipping.

questions.prompt: Why does RLHF train the reward model on pairwise rankings instead of absolute quality scores?
options: Pairwise rankings are cheaper to compute automatically
Absolute scores are illegal to collect from crowdworkers
Humans are much more consistent when comparing two outputs than when rating one on an absolute scale
Pairwise data doesn't require a Bradley-Terry loss
questions.explanation: Absolute 1–10 style ratings vary a lot between labelers and even for the same labeler over time. 'Which of these two is better' is a far more reliable, reproducible judgment — which is why the reward model is trained with a Bradley-Terry-style pairwise loss.

posts.title: PagedAttention: Serving LLMs Without Wasting the KV Cache
posts.subtitle: vLLM's trick: treat the KV cache like OS virtual memory, not one giant reserved block.
posts.summary: PagedAttention applies OS-style virtual memory paging to the LLM KV cache, splitting it into fixed-size blocks instead of one contiguous reservation per request. It cut wasted KV-cache memory from 60-80% down to under 4% and is now the default memory manager behind most production LLM serving stacks.

slides.title: The KV cache used to waste 60-80% of its allocated memory
slides.body: PagedAttention, introduced by the vLLM team (UC Berkeley, Stanford, UC San Diego, 2023), applies OS-style virtual memory paging to the attention KV cache — and it's now the default memory manager behind most production LLM serving stacks.
bullets: From the vLLM paper (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023)
Fixes fragmentation in how servers store each request's KV cache
Now standard in vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and most serving frameworks

slides.title: Contiguous KV cache allocation wastes most of the memory
slides.body: Before PagedAttention, servers reserved one contiguous memory block per request sized for the maximum possible sequence length — even for a 10-token prompt.
bullets: A request generating 20 tokens still reserves memory for the max possible length 'just in case'
Internal fragmentation: unused reserved space inside a request's own block
External fragmentation: gaps between blocks too small to fit a new request
Measured result: 60-80% of KV cache memory wasted this way

slides.title: Borrow paging from operating systems
slides.body: PagedAttention splits each sequence's KV cache into fixed-size blocks (like OS memory pages) that don't need to be contiguous in GPU memory.
bullets: KV cache split into small fixed-size blocks, each holding a handful of tokens
A block table (like a page table) maps logical sequence positions to physical GPU blocks
Blocks are allocated on demand as generation proceeds — no upfront max-length reservation

slides.title: What this unlocks beyond saving memory
slides.body: Once the cache is block-based, sharing memory across requests becomes possible.
bullets: Copy-on-write blocks let parallel sampling (multiple completions from one prompt) share the prompt's KV cache instead of duplicating it
Beam search shares cache blocks across beams that haven't diverged yet
Memory that used to sit reserved-but-unused goes directly into a bigger batch size

slides.title: The numbers from the original paper

rows: 2-4x higher at the same latency target

slides.title: A worked example: 3 requests sharing a GPU
slides.body: How the pieces combine in practice.
bullets: Request A: a 10-token prompt wants a 20-token reply — old systems reserve a slab sized for the max sequence length; PagedAttention allocates just a couple of blocks and grows them as needed
Request B: same prompt as A, but samples 4 parallel completions — the shared prompt's blocks are copy-on-write across all 4, instead of duplicated 4x
Net effect: many more concurrent requests fit in the same GPU memory, which is what drives the throughput gain

slides.title: Where paging isn't free
slides.body: The technique has real tradeoffs, not just upside.
bullets: Block-table lookups add a small indirection cost per attention step vs. a flat contiguous cache
Custom attention kernels are required to read efficiently from non-contiguous block memory
Very short, fixed-length workloads (e.g. classification) see less benefit — there's little fragmentation to fix

slides.title: What to actually take from this
bullets: PagedAttention treats the KV cache like OS virtual memory: fixed-size blocks plus a block table, not one giant reservation
Fixing fragmentation is what lets serving frameworks pack more concurrent requests onto the same GPU
Copy-on-write block sharing is what makes parallel sampling and beam search cheap
It's now table-stakes: most production LLM servers ship some form of paged KV cache

questions.prompt: What problem does PagedAttention solve in LLM serving?
options: Slow tokenization
Memory fragmentation from over-reserving contiguous KV cache space
Overfitting during fine-tuning
Slow disk I/O when loading model weights
questions.explanation: Before PagedAttention, servers reserved one contiguous block sized for the max possible sequence length per request, wasting 60-80% of that memory to internal and external fragmentation.

questions.prompt: What OS concept does PagedAttention borrow to fix this?
options: Process scheduling
Virtual memory paging with fixed-size blocks and a block/page table
File system journaling
Interrupt handling
questions.explanation: PagedAttention splits the KV cache into fixed-size blocks that don't need to be contiguous in memory, tracked with a block table — the same idea as OS virtual memory paging.

questions.prompt: Why does block-based KV cache make parallel sampling cheaper?
options: It skips computing attention for extra samples entirely
Shared prompt blocks can be copy-on-write across multiple completions instead of duplicated per sample
It reduces the number of tokens generated
It stores samples on disk instead of GPU memory
questions.explanation: Because the KV cache is block-based, multiple completions sampled from the same prompt can share that prompt's blocks via copy-on-write, only duplicating memory once the sequences actually diverge.

posts.title: SMELT: Loop the Middle Layers, Skip the Bigger Model
posts.subtitle: Looping half a MoE transformer's layers twice cuts training compute 6.8–18% at matched size.
posts.summary: SMELT (Tsinghua + ByteDance) is the first looped-transformer study to hold FLOPs, parameters, and KV-cache fixed against a non-looped baseline. Looping just the middle half of a MoE transformer's layers twice cuts compute-optimal training FLOPs by 6.8-18%, with gains concentrated on code and long-context tasks.

slides.title: A transformer that revisits its own middle layers
slides.body: SMELT, from researchers at Tsinghua University and ByteDance, re-runs the middle half of a Mixture-of-Experts transformer's layers a second time — and does it under a strict apples-to-apples compute comparison most looped-architecture papers skip.
bullets: Posted to arXiv September 2026 (2609.01343)
Loops the middle half of layers twice, matching baseline compute/params/KV-cache
Cuts compute-optimal training FLOPs by 6.8-18%

slides.title: Depth used to mean more layers. That's not free.
slides.body: Most prior looped-transformer papers compared architectures at a fixed parameter count — which quietly hands the looped model extra FLOPs per token, since it runs some layers twice. That makes 'looping helps' hard to distinguish from 'looping just spends more compute.'
bullets: Fixed-parameter comparisons conflate architectural gains with extra FLOPs
A looped model with more compute beating the baseline proves little
SMELT is the first to match FLOPs, non-embedding params, AND KV-cache simultaneously

slides.title: The recipe: loop only the middle, only twice
slides.body: SMELT stands for Sparse MoE Transformer, middle-layers-Loop-Twice. Instead of looping the whole stack, it re-runs just the middle 50% of layers one extra time, while holding total non-embedding parameters, per-token FLOPs, and KV-cache size fixed against a matched non-looped baseline.
bullets: Loops the middle half of layers exactly one extra pass (not the full stack)
Held constant vs. baseline: non-embedding params, per-token FLOPs, KV-cache size
Scaled across four model sizes up to 54B non-embedding parameters
A separate Chinchilla-style scaling law fit for each architecture

slides.title: What compute-matching actually bought
slides.body: At every scale and sparsity level tested, SMELT reached lower validation loss than the matched baseline — and the advantage carried over to downstream benchmarks, not just the loss curve.

rows: Grows with longer samples and more in-context examples

slides.title: What looping actually changes inside the model
slides.body: The paper doesn't stop at the loss curve — it looks at attention patterns to explain why the second pass helps.
bullets: On the second visit through looped layers, the attention sink (heavy attention on token 0) shrinks
That freed attention mass gets redirected toward content-relevant tokens
Reads as a refinement step — like re-reading a draft — not just bolted-on extra capacity

slides.title: Where this stops paying off
slides.body: Compute-matched training FLOPs is not the same as free inference — and the results are still lab-scale.
bullets: The extra pass adds inference latency even though parameters stay fixed — a real throughput cost
Gains concentrate on code and long-context settings; smaller on short, simple prompts
Tested only up to 54B non-embedding params — not yet validated at 100B+ frontier scale

slides.title: What to actually take from this
bullets: Match FLOPs, params, and KV-cache before claiming an architecture 'wins' — that framing is the paper's real contribution
Looping trades inference latency for training-compute savings, not a free upgrade
Looping just the middle half, twice, beats naively looping the whole stack at matched budget
The effect is mechanistic (attention-sink reduction), not just a curve fit

questions.prompt: What is the key methodological fix SMELT makes compared to prior looped-transformer studies?
options: It uses a much bigger model than any baseline
It matches compute (FLOPs), parameters, and KV-cache against a non-looped baseline
It removes the KV cache entirely
It trains on more data than the baseline
questions.explanation: Prior comparisons matched parameter count but let looped models use more FLOPs per token, which made looping look better partly because it was more expensive. SMELT holds FLOPs, params, and KV-cache fixed to isolate the real architectural effect.

questions.prompt: Which layers does SMELT loop, and how many extra times?
options: All layers, three extra passes
The middle half of layers, one extra pass
Only the first layer, five extra passes
The output layer only, one extra pass
questions.explanation: SMELT ('middle layers Loop Twice') re-runs just the middle 50% of the network one extra time, rather than looping the whole stack or a single layer.

questions.prompt: According to the paper's mechanistic analysis, what changes on the second pass through the looped layers?
options: The model attends more heavily to the first token (attention sink) for stability
Attention sink shrinks and attention mass shifts toward content-relevant tokens
The KV cache doubles in size
Gradient updates are skipped entirely on the second pass
questions.explanation: The second visit reduces the attention sink and redirects that freed attention toward tokens that carry real information — evidence the loop acts as a refinement step, not just extra raw capacity.
