posts.title: Qwen-Drive-1.0: One VLM That Sees, Answers, and Drives
posts.subtitle: Alibaba's Qwen team folds 3D perception and trajectory planning into a single vision-language model.
posts.summary: Qwen-Drive-1.0 keeps a pretrained vision-language model's architecture intact and bolts on a bird's-eye-view perception head and a planning head, so one model handles 3D detection, visual Q&A, and trajectory generation. It beats specialist baselines on nuScenes and shows RL fine-tuning helps planning metrics — but not every metric.

slides.title: Driving stacks are usually a pipeline. This is one model.
slides.body: arXiv 2609.00111, posted August 31, 2026, by the Qwen Team at Alibaba. Code and weights are public on GitHub.
bullets: Built on the Qwen3.5-4B vision-language backbone
Unifies perception, VQA, and planning in one forward pass
Open-sourced under QwenLM/Qwen-Drive-1.0

slides.title: Why bolt driving onto a chat model at all?
slides.body: Most self-driving stacks stitch together separate perception, prediction, and planning modules. That loses the causal reasoning a VLM already has — 'the pedestrian is looking at their phone, so brake early' isn't a detection box, it's an inference.
bullets: Pure VQA adaptation of a VLM keeps reasoning but loses precise 3D grounding
Pure perception stacks keep precision but can't explain 'why'
Qwen-Drive-1.0 tries to keep both in one shared representation

slides.title: Two heads bolted onto one shared backbone
slides.body: The VLM backbone stays untouched. A bird's-eye-view (BEV) perception head handles 3D object detection, semantic occupancy, and map segmentation; a separate Planning Expert head consumes the same VLM representations to output future ego trajectories.
bullets: Staged training: driving supervision mixed with general VQA data
General VQA data is kept in the mix specifically to avoid catastrophic forgetting of instruction-following
Same shared features feed both perception and planning heads

slides.title: nuScenes: beating specialist perception baselines
slides.body: The SFT variant sets new state-of-the-art numbers against dedicated BEV perception models, despite the backbone being a general-purpose VLM.

slides.title: Worked example: planning score in practice
slides.body: On NAVSIM v1.1 navtest, measured by the PDMS driving-quality metric, the SFT model scores 88.2 (89.3 best-of-6 samples). After RL fine-tuning, that climbs to 90.7 (91.4 best-of-6) — a real, measurable planning improvement from reinforcement learning on top of supervised fine-tuning.
bullets: Waymo Open Dataset end-to-end RFS score: 7.78 (SFT) → 7.91 (RL)
Both benchmarks move in the same direction after RL
RL is applied on top of the SFT checkpoint, not from scratch

slides.title: The catch: RL doesn't win on every axis
slides.body: On NVIDIA's PhysicalAI open-loop benchmark (minADE at 3 seconds), the RL model actually scores worse than SFT: 0.38m vs. 0.34m. Optimizing for one planning reward can trade off against raw trajectory accuracy elsewhere.
bullets: Lower minADE is better — RL regressed here while improving PDMS and RFS
A reminder that RL reward shaping optimizes what you measure, not everything at once
The authors themselves call this 'an initial step,' not a finished driving stack

slides.title: What this paper actually establishes
bullets: A single VLM backbone can match or beat specialist BEV perception models
RL on top of SFT measurably improves some planning metrics — PDMS and RFS both rose
But RL fine-tuning isn't free: minADE got worse on a separate benchmark
Open weights + code (QwenLM/Qwen-Drive-1.0) make this directly reproducible, unlike most driving-stack papers

options: A speech head and a translation head
A bird's-eye-view perception head and a planning head
Two identical perception heads for redundancy
A text-only head and an image-only head

questions.prompt: On the NVIDIA PhysicalAI open-loop benchmark, how did the RL-tuned model compare to the SFT model?

RL was identical to SFT on all benchmarks
RL improved PDMS and RFS but scored worse on minADE
RL was never evaluated on PhysicalAI

It's required by the benchmark rules
To avoid catastrophic forgetting of the VLM's instruction-following and reasoning ability
It has no effect and is included only as a baseline

posts.title: Embeddings: Turning Words Into Numbers a Machine Can Compare
posts.subtitle: Every RAG pipeline, semantic search bar, and recommendation engine starts here.
posts.summary: An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so a computer can measure how similar two ideas are by comparing vectors instead of matching characters. That single trick underlies semantic search, RAG retrieval, and recommendation systems.

slides.title: Computers can't tell 'dog' and 'puppy' are related — unless you help them
slides.body: String comparison sees two unrelated sequences of letters. Embeddings turn text into vectors so 'related meaning' becomes 'nearby points in space.'
bullets: The foundation under every semantic search and RAG system
Turns 'similar meaning' into 'similar numbers'

slides.title: Why exact matching falls apart fast
slides.body: A keyword search for 'car problems' will miss a document that only says 'my vehicle won't start.' No shared substrings, but obviously the same topic.
bullets: Synonyms, paraphrases, and typos all break exact-match search
Keyword search needs the same words; meaning search needs the same idea
This gap is exactly what embeddings close

slides.title: What an embedding actually is
slides.body: A neural network maps a piece of text to a fixed-length list of numbers — say, 1536 floating-point values. Texts with similar meaning end up as vectors that point in similar directions.
bullets: Trained with contrastive learning: pull matching pairs' vectors together, push mismatched pairs apart
Similarity is usually measured with cosine similarity: 1.0 = identical direction, 0 = unrelated, −1 = opposite
The vector itself isn't interpretable — no single number means 'sports' — the pattern across all of them does

slides.title: Worked example: three sentences, one comparison
slides.body: Embed three sentences and compare each pair with cosine similarity. Meaning clusters together even when the words don't overlap at all.

rows: "The cat sat on the mat" vs "A feline rested on the rug"
"The cat sat on the mat" vs "The stock market fell today"
"The cat sat on the mat" vs "The cat sat on the mat."

slides.title: Not all embedding models are the same size
slides.body: Dimension count is a real design tradeoff: bigger vectors usually capture more nuance but cost more to store and compare at scale.

slides.title: Where embeddings quietly break things
slides.body: Embeddings are powerful but not magic — two mistakes cause most production bugs.
bullets: Never mix vectors from two different embedding models in one index — their spaces aren't compatible, similarity scores become meaningless
Switching embedding models means re-embedding your entire corpus, not just new documents
Pure embedding search can still miss exact matches (IDs, error codes, acronyms) — that gap is why hybrid keyword+vector search exists

slides.title: The core idea, compressed
bullets: An embedding is a fixed-length vector that encodes meaning, not just words
Cosine similarity turns 'how related are these?' into a single number between −1 and 1
Bigger dimension counts trade cost for nuance — pick based on your scale, not just accuracy leaderboards
Never mix embedding models in the same index; re-embed everything when you switch

questions.prompt: What does an embedding model actually output for a piece of text?
options: A shortened summary of the text
A fixed-length vector of numbers representing meaning
A list of the most important keywords
A translated version of the text
questions.explanation: An embedding is a fixed-length numeric vector. Texts with similar meaning produce vectors that point in similar directions, even if they share no words.

questions.prompt: Two sentences with a cosine similarity near 1.0 most likely have:
options: Completely unrelated meanings
Very similar or identical meaning
The exact same number of words
No relationship — cosine similarity is random
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity near 1.0 means the two vectors point in nearly the same direction in embedding space, which corresponds to very similar meaning.

questions.prompt: Why can't you mix vectors from two different embedding models in the same search index?
options: It's technically fine and commonly done in production
Different models produce incompatible vector spaces, so similarity comparisons become meaningless
It would only slow down search speed, not affect accuracy
Embedding models all produce the same vector space by design
questions.explanation: Each embedding model learns its own geometry during training. A vector from one model has no reliable spatial relationship to a vector from a different model, so comparing them produces meaningless similarity scores.

posts.title: Consistent Hashing: Scaling a Cluster Without Reshuffling Everything
posts.subtitle: Naive mod-N hashing remaps almost every key when a node joins or leaves — one ring-shaped trick fixes that.
posts.summary: Naive key%N sharding remaps nearly every key whenever a node is added or removed, forcing a mass cache miss or data migration. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on the same circular hash space so only the keys owned by the changed node's neighbors move — roughly 1/N of the data instead of nearly all of it. Virtual nodes fix the uneven-load problem that a plain ring introduces, at the cost of extra bookkeeping.

slides.title: Adding One Server Shouldn't Move Everyone's Data
slides.body: Consistent hashing is the technique behind distributed caches, sharded databases, and CDNs that lets clusters grow and shrink without a full data reshuffle.
bullets: Used in Amazon's Dynamo, Apache Cassandra, DynamoDB, and memcached client libraries
Solves one specific problem: minimizing key movement when the number of nodes changes
The core idea is a hash ring — nodes and keys share the same circular coordinate space

slides.title: Naive hash(key) % N Breaks the Moment N Changes
slides.body: The obvious way to shard is key % numberOfNodes. It's simple and balances load perfectly — right up until a node joins or leaves.
bullets: Going from N to N+1 nodes changes the modulus for almost every key, not just the new node's share
A key that mapped to bucket 7 under %10 can land on a completely different bucket under %11
In practice this means nearly the entire cache goes cold, or nearly the entire dataset gets re-copied, on a single scaling event
That's unacceptable for a live cache or a database that can't afford a full re-shard window

slides.title: Put Nodes and Keys on the Same Ring
slides.body: Consistent hashing hashes both the nodes and the keys into one large circular space (commonly 0 to 2^32-1) and assigns each key to the first node found walking clockwise.
bullets: Hash each node's identifier (e.g. its IP:port) onto the ring — that's its position
Hash each key the same way, then walk clockwise to find the nearest node — that node owns the key
When a node is removed, only the keys between it and its counter-clockwise neighbor move — they now belong to that neighbor
When a node is added, it only steals keys from the single node it lands next to on the ring

slides.title: Virtual Nodes Fix the Ring's Load-Balance Problem
slides.body: A plain ring with one point per physical node produces wildly uneven arcs by chance — one node might own 40% of the keyspace while another owns 5%.
bullets: The fix: hash each physical node to many points on the ring (its 'virtual nodes'), not just one
More virtual nodes per physical node smooths out the arc sizes, converging toward an even split
Virtual nodes also make heterogeneous hardware easy: give a bigger machine more virtual nodes to give it a proportionally bigger share
The tradeoff is memory and lookup cost — every virtual node is an entry the router has to keep and search

slides.title: Keys Remapped When the Cluster Changes Size
slides.body: This is the entire reason consistent hashing exists: it bounds how much data moves on a topology change.

rows: Poor — arcs vary widely by chance
Good — smooths out with more virtual points
Good, no ring bookkeeping, but O(N) lookup per key

slides.title: Worked Example: Growing a 4-Node Cache to 5
slides.body: Say a memcached cluster holds 1,000,000 keys across 4 nodes on a consistent-hash ring.
bullets: Naive mod-N: switching from %4 to %5 relocates on the order of 800,000+ keys — almost the whole cache goes cold at once
Consistent hashing: the new 5th node's virtual points carve arcs out of its ring neighbors only — roughly 200,000 keys (about 1/5) move, the other 800,000 stay exactly where they were
Those 800,000 untouched keys mean the other 4 nodes keep serving cache hits through the whole rebalance
Only the new node and its immediate neighbors need to stream data during the transition — not the whole cluster

slides.title: Where It Bites: Hotspots and Skewed Keys
slides.body: Consistent hashing bounds churn, but it doesn't guarantee even load if your access pattern is skewed.
bullets: A single viral key (a celebrity profile, a trending post) can still overload whichever one node owns it — consistent hashing spreads storage, not per-key traffic
Too few virtual nodes per physical node still leaves lumpy arcs; too many bloats the routing table every client must hold
Ring position isn't capacity-aware by default — a small node and a large node get equal shares unless you deliberately assign more virtual nodes to the bigger one
Not worth the complexity for a fixed, rarely-resized cluster — plain mod-N sharding is simpler and fine if node count never changes

slides.title: The Core Trade Being Made
slides.body: Consistent hashing swaps a small amount of routing complexity for a huge reduction in data movement during scaling events.
bullets: Naive hashing: simple, but a node change reshuffles nearly everything
Consistent hashing: a node change moves roughly 1/N of the keys, bounded and predictable
Virtual nodes trade extra ring entries for even load distribution and capacity-aware sharding
It solves data placement, not hot-key traffic — pair it with request-level caching or replication for viral keys

questions.prompt: A cluster shards keys with hash(key) % N. Why is adding one more node so disruptive?
options: It changes the modulus, which remaps almost every key to a different bucket, not just a share of them
It doubles memory usage on every node
It requires re-hashing every node's identifier
It only affects keys that hash to the new node's exact bucket number
questions.explanation: Because % N depends on the total node count, changing N changes where nearly every key lands — not a targeted subset. That's the exact problem consistent hashing was designed to avoid.

questions.prompt: In consistent hashing, when a node is removed from the ring, which keys move?
options: All keys in the cluster
Only the keys that were owned by the removed node — they pass to its next clockwise neighbor
No keys move; removal is free
Every key whose hash is a multiple of the node count
questions.explanation: Only the arc previously owned by the removed node changes hands, going to its neighbor on the ring. Every other node's keys are untouched, which is exactly why the disruption is bounded to roughly 1/N of the data.

questions.prompt: Why do real systems give each physical node many 'virtual nodes' on the ring instead of just one?
options: It makes hashing faster
It's required for the ring to work at all
A single point per node produces unevenly sized arcs by chance; many points per node average out into a fairer split, and let bigger machines get proportionally more virtual nodes
It removes the need to hash keys
questions.explanation: With only one ring position per node, arc sizes vary widely by luck of the hash. Spreading each physical node across many virtual positions smooths that out, and assigning more virtual nodes to higher-capacity machines lets the ring reflect real capacity differences.

posts.title: LoRA: Fine-Tuning Billion-Parameter Models on a Single GPU
posts.subtitle: Freeze the weights, train a tiny low-rank patch instead — most of full fine-tuning's quality for a fraction of the memory.
posts.summary: LoRA freezes a pretrained model's weights and learns a small low-rank correction matrix instead of updating every parameter. It cuts trainable parameters and optimizer memory by orders of magnitude, merges back into the base model for free at inference, and — combined with 4-bit quantization as QLoRA — lets a 65B model be fine-tuned on a single GPU.

slides.title: Fine-Tuning Without Touching Most of the Model
slides.body: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes a pretrained model's weights and trains a tiny add-on patch instead of the whole network.
bullets: The base model's weights never change — a small correction matrix is learned alongside them
Trainable parameters typically drop to under 1% of the full model
The patch merges back into the base weights after training, adding zero inference latency

slides.title: Full Fine-Tuning Costs 4x a Model's Weight Memory
slides.body: The Adam optimizer is the hidden cost: every trainable parameter needs its weight, its gradient, and two optimizer moment buffers held in memory simultaneously.
bullets: A 7B-parameter model in fp16 is already about 14GB of weights alone
Full fine-tuning with Adam needs weights + gradients + 2 moment buffers — well over 100GB before a single batch loads
That memory bill rules out fine-tuning on a single consumer or even single-datacenter GPU

slides.title: Freeze W, Learn a Low-Rank Update ΔW = B·A
slides.body: LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) replaces 'update every weight' with 'learn a small correction.' The original weight matrix W never moves.
bullets: For a weight matrix W (size d×k), LoRA adds two small matrices B (d×r) and A (r×k), where rank r is often just 4-16
Only B and A get gradients — W stays frozen throughout training
B is initialized to all zeros, so ΔW = B·A = 0 on step one — training starts exactly at the base model's behavior
A scaling factor (alpha/r) controls how strongly the learned update is applied once training moves it away from zero

slides.title: Usually Bolted Onto the Attention Projections
slides.body: You choose which weight matrices get a LoRA adapter — adapting the whole model isn't required.
bullets: Most setups target the query and value projections (Wq, Wv) in attention; some also adapt key/output projections and MLP layers
More target matrices means more adaptation capacity, but more trainable parameters and memory to train
Because ΔW = B·A merges algebraically into W, the adapter can be folded into the base weights after training with zero added inference cost
Unmerged adapters can also be kept separate and hot-swapped per task or customer without duplicating the full base model

slides.title: Worked Example: 7B Model, 24GB GPU
slides.body: The original LoRA paper fine-tuned GPT-3 175B with 10,000x fewer trainable parameters and 3x less GPU memory than full fine-tuning.
bullets: Full fine-tune of a 7B model (fp16 weights + fp32 Adam states): well over 100GB of GPU memory, needing multiple GPUs
LoRA at rank r=8 on Wq/Wv across every layer: roughly 4-8M trainable parameters — under 0.1% of the 7B total
That collapse in optimizer-state memory is what makes fine-tuning fit on a single 24GB consumer GPU
QLoRA goes further: quantize the frozen base model to 4-bit (NF4) and train LoRA adapters on top of it — a 65B model fine-tunes on one 48GB GPU

slides.title: Trainable Parameters vs. Inference Cost
slides.body: These methods trade off differently — LoRA's specific advantage is paying almost nothing extra at inference time.

rows: Extra tokens on every forward pass
Same as LoRA, on a 4-bit base

slides.title: Rank Is a Dial, Not a Free Lunch
slides.body: LoRA doesn't reduce training compute — the full forward and backward pass still runs through the frozen base model. It only shrinks trainable parameters and optimizer memory.
bullets: Too small a rank (r=1-2) underfits tasks that need broad behavior change, like teaching a genuinely new skill or language
Forward/backward FLOPs through the frozen base model are unchanged — LoRA saves memory and storage, not training wall-clock
Serving many unmerged adapters per request adds latency and routing complexity versus one merged model
Catastrophic forgetting still happens, just less severely than full fine-tuning, since most of the network stays frozen

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: LoRA freezes the base weights and learns a low-rank correction B·A instead of updating every parameter
It cuts trainable parameters and optimizer memory by orders of magnitude — not training compute
The adapter merges back into the base model for free at inference; QLoRA adds 4-bit quantization for even bigger memory savings
Pick rank and target layers based on how much the task actually needs to change the model's behavior

questions.prompt: What does LoRA actually train?
options: Every weight in the model
A pair of small low-rank matrices added to selected weight matrices
Only the embedding layer
A separate reward model
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes the original weight matrix W and learns a low-rank decomposition B·A added to it — only B and A receive gradients.

questions.prompt: Why is the B matrix initialized to all zeros?
options: To save disk space
So the model matches the frozen base model's output exactly before any training happens
Because A is initialized to zero instead
It's an unrelated regularization trick
questions.explanation: With B=0, ΔW = B·A = 0 at step one, so training starts from the exact same behavior as the untouched base model and only diverges as B learns.

questions.prompt: What does LoRA NOT save you, compared to full fine-tuning?
options: GPU memory for optimizer states
Disk space for storing many fine-tuned variants
Forward/backward compute through the frozen base model
Trainable parameter count
questions.explanation: LoRA still runs a full forward and backward pass through the frozen base model each step — it reduces trainable parameters and optimizer memory, not the FLOPs spent per training step.

posts.title: Claude Mythos 5.1: The Model Anthropic Won't Hand You
posts.subtitle: Same weights as Fable 5.1, permissive safeguards — and access gated to vetted cyber and biology labs only.
posts.summary: Anthropic released Claude Mythos 5.1 alongside Claude Fable 5.1 on September 1, 2026 — the same underlying model, but run with its cyber safeguards relaxed. It posts the strongest cyber benchmark of any Anthropic model (60.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0) and designs high-affinity protein binders at nearly 5x the typical industry hit rate, but stays restricted to vetted professionals through two verification programs rather than shipping as a public API.

slides.title: One Model, Two Names, One Locked Door
bullets: Released September 1, 2026 alongside the general-availability Claude Fable 5.1
Mythos 5.1 is the same weights as Fable 5.1, run with cyber safeguards deliberately relaxed
Access restricted to vetted organizations via Anthropic's Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs

slides.title: Why Gate a Model Instead of Just Shipping It
slides.body: The same capability that lets a model find and patch a vulnerability, or design a novel protein, can just as easily be pointed the other way.
bullets: Cyber offense and cyber defense draw on the same underlying skill — better vulnerability-finding helps both
A model that designs high-affinity protein binders for medicine can, in principle, be asked to design harmful ones instead
Anthropic's answer: keep one capability level, but gate who gets to run it with weaker guardrails

slides.title: What Actually Changes Between Fable and Mythos
slides.body: Fable 5.1 ships generally available as claude-fable-5-1. Mythos 5.1 is the identical model, but evaluated and deployed with its cybersecurity intervention layer loosened for approved users.
bullets: Cyber Verification Program: vets security researchers, red teams, and defenders before granting Mythos access
Life Sciences Verification Program: separately vets biology and biosecurity-adjacent researchers
Both programs sit under Anthropic's Frontier Compliance Framework, which classifies model risk tiers before release

slides.title: The Numbers Behind the Gate
bullets: The 5-point Terminal-Bench gap between Fable and Mythos is entirely the safeguard difference — same weights, same training run
Pricing didn't move for the capability jump: cache reads got cheaper, base rates held

slides.title: Worked Case: Designing a Protein Binder
slides.body: In Adaptyv Bio's independent protein-design competitions, Anthropic tested Mythos on the kind of task a biosecurity-sensitive model needs to be good — and safe — at.
bullets: Task: design a high-affinity binder molecule for a target protein, submitted blind against other entrants
Typical industry hit rate for a working high-affinity binder: 10-15%
Mythos 5.1's hit rate: nearly 50% — close to 5x the usual success rate
That same competence is exactly why access is vetted rather than public

slides.title: 'Lower Risk' Is a Classification, Not a Guarantee
slides.body: Even with cyber safeguards off, Anthropic places Mythos 5.1 in the lower-risk tier of its own Frontier Compliance Framework — a self-assessment, not an independent audit.
bullets: Anthropic states Mythos 5.1 shows the strongest cyber capabilities of any model it has released
The lower-risk classification comes from Anthropic's internal framework — no third-party audit of the risk tiering was disclosed
Verification-gated release (seen here and in Google's Gemini Cyber line) is becoming the default pattern for dual-use frontier capability, not a one-off

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Mythos 5.1 and Fable 5.1 are the same model — the difference is which safeguards are switched on for whom
60.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 is the highest cyber-relevant score Anthropic has published for any of its models
Protein-binder design at ~50% hit rate (vs. 10-15% industry norm) shows the same jump shows up in biology, not just code
Expect verification-gated releases to become standard whenever a model's top capability is dual-use

posts.title: AlphaProof Nexus: Solving Erdős Problems for a Few Hundred Dollars
posts.subtitle: DeepMind pairs an LLM with the Lean proof checker and lets an agent loop grind on open math problems until Lean says yes.
posts.summary: Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus fuses an LLM with the Lean formal proof assistant in an autonomous agent loop, resolving 9 of 353 open Erdős problems and 44 of 492 open OEIS conjectures at roughly $100-500 in inference cost per problem. Every proof is a machine-checked Lean certificate published on GitHub — a rare AI math result that doesn't require trusting the model's own claims.

slides.title: An Agent That Has to Prove Its Work
bullets: Google DeepMind, arXiv 2605.22763, submitted May 21 2026
Pairs an LLM (Gemini) with the Lean formal proof assistant in an autonomous agentic loop
Resolved 9/353 open Erdős problems and 44/492 open OEIS conjectures — each one a machine-checked proof

slides.title: LLMs Are Fluent at Math. That's the Problem.
slides.body: A model can write a proof that reads perfectly and is still wrong — natural-language 'proofs' have no automatic way to be checked.
bullets: Grading LLM math output usually means trusting the model, a human reviewer, or another LLM as judge
Formal proof languages like Lean remove that trust problem — a proof either compiles against the Lean kernel or it doesn't
The catch: writing Lean by hand is slow, specialized work most researchers avoid for exploratory problems

slides.title: Generate, Compile, Retry
slides.body: AlphaProof Nexus isn't one-shot generation — it's a loop: the LLM proposes a proof step in Lean, the Lean kernel compiles or rejects it, and the failure feeds back into the next attempt.
bullets: The kernel — not a grader model or a human — is the source of truth for every step
Four variants were compared to isolate what actually helps: a basic LLM+Lean loop, +AlphaProof search, +evolutionary search, and the full combined system
Stronger, more expensive models handle complex proof steps; cheaper models rank and filter draft candidates at high throughput

slides.title: Which Component Actually Earns Its Cost
slides.body: The surprising finding: on easy problems, the stripped-down basic loop was the most cost-efficient — the extra machinery only pays off once problems get hard.
bullets: The basic LLM+Lean loop alone solved all 9 Erdős problems in a post-hoc re-run
On the two hardest problems (Erdős #125 and #138), the full system was 2-5x more cost-efficient than the basic loop at the same solve rate

rows: Cheapest per solve on easy-to-medium problems
Mutates and recombines partial proof attempts
Better survival on longer proof chains
2-5x more cost-efficient on the two hardest problems

slides.title: What 9 Solved Problems Actually Looks Like
slides.body: The results weren't confined to Erdős's list — the same agent loop crossed into other open areas of math.
bullets: Two of the Erdős problems had sat unresolved for 56 years before the agent cracked them
It resolved a 15-year-old open question in algebraic geometry involving Hilbert functions
It improved a known bound in convex optimization by discovering a novel algorithmic parameter schedule
It contributed to closing a problem from Ben Green's well-known list of open conjectures

slides.title: What It Can't Do — and Why the Cost Number Matters
slides.body: Each proof cost roughly $100-500 in inference — dramatically cheaper than the researcher-hours it would otherwise take, but the system is bounded by what Lean can check.
bullets: It doesn't originate new conjectures — it searches for proofs of problems already stated in formal terms
A problem that can't be cleanly formalized in Lean is outside its reach entirely
Because every result compiles against the Lean kernel and is published on GitHub, no one has to trust DeepMind's claims — the proofs are independently, mechanically checkable

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: AlphaProof Nexus = LLM proposal + Lean kernel verification, run as an iterative agent loop, not single-shot generation
9/353 Erdős problems and 44/492 OEIS conjectures solved, each backed by a machine-checked proof anyone can compile
Extra search machinery (AlphaProof + evolution) only pays for itself on the hardest problems — simpler is cheaper on easy ones
The real innovation isn't 'AI does math' — it's coupling generation to a checker that can't be fooled

questions.prompt: Why does AlphaProof Nexus use the Lean proof assistant instead of just trusting the LLM's own proof text?
options: Lean makes the LLM run faster
Lean's kernel mechanically compiles or rejects each proof step, so correctness doesn't depend on trusting the model
Lean is required by arXiv for math papers
Lean generates the proofs itself, without an LLM
questions.explanation: A fluent natural-language 'proof' can be wrong with no automatic way to check it. Lean's kernel gives a ground truth: a proof either compiles against the target statement or it doesn't.

questions.prompt: What did comparing the four agent variants (basic, +AlphaProof, +evolution, full) reveal?
options: The full system was always the cheapest option, on every problem
The basic LLM+Lean loop alone solved all 9 Erdős problems and was cheapest on easy ones; the extra machinery only paid off on the hardest problems
Evolutionary search alone outperformed every other variant
None of the variants could solve more than 2 problems total
questions.explanation: The basic loop matched the full system's solve count on the 9 Erdős problems in post-hoc analysis and was more cost-efficient on easier ones. The full system's advantage — 2-5x better cost-efficiency — only showed up on the two hardest problems.

questions.prompt: What is a real limitation of AlphaProof Nexus, according to the paper?
options: It cannot run on any open-source Lean library
It can only search for proofs of problems already stated formally in Lean — it doesn't originate new conjectures
It requires a human to manually check every generated proof
It only works on algebra problems, not geometry or optimization
questions.explanation: The system searches a proof space Lean can verify for a problem someone has already formalized. It doesn't propose new open questions — a meaningfully different and still-unsolved capability.

posts.title: Knowledge Distillation: Training a Small Model to Think Like a Big One
posts.subtitle: The technique behind every 'mini' model that punches above its parameter count — teach it the teacher's uncertainty, not just its answers.
posts.summary: Knowledge distillation trains a small 'student' model to match a large 'teacher' model's full output distribution, not just its final answer. That extra signal — the teacher's relative confidence across wrong answers — is why distilled models often beat same-sized models trained from scratch, and why so many small models today trace their reasoning ability back to a much larger one.

slides.title: Two Models, One Lesson Plan
bullets: A large, expensive 'teacher' model generates training signal for a small, cheap 'student' model
The student doesn't just copy final answers — it learns the teacher's full probability distribution over possible outputs
The result: a model a fraction of the size that keeps most of the teacher's competence on the tasks it was distilled for

slides.title: Frontier Capability, Non-Frontier Budget
slides.body: The best models are big, slow, and expensive to serve at scale — often too costly to run on-device or at the request volume a product actually needs.
bullets: Serving a 400B-parameter model for every user request doesn't fit a phone, a browser extension, or a tight latency budget
Training a small model from scratch on the same data rarely reaches the same quality — it's missing the teacher's learned structure
You want the teacher's judgment baked into something small enough to actually deploy

slides.title: The Trick: Soft Labels, Not Hard Labels
slides.body: Training on hard labels only tells the student 'this is the right answer.' Training on the teacher's softened output distribution tells it how confident the teacher was in every wrong answer too.
bullets: The teacher's logits are divided by a temperature T before the softmax, spreading probability mass across near-miss answers
The student is trained to minimize KL-divergence between its own softened distribution and the teacher's
That relative-confidence signal — sometimes called 'dark knowledge' — carries structure a single correct label can't

slides.title: Three Flavors of Distillation
slides.body: Matching final output isn't the only option — what gets matched between teacher and student varies by method.
bullets: Response-based: student trains on the teacher's generated text or reasoning traces — the dominant approach for today's LLMs
Feature-based: student matches the teacher's intermediate hidden states or attention patterns, not just outputs
Relation-based: student learns to preserve how the teacher relates different examples to each other, not each one in isolation

slides.title: Distillation vs. the Other Ways to Shrink a Model
bullets: These three techniques are often combined, not chosen exclusively — a distilled student can later be quantized too

rows: Parameter count — a genuinely new, smaller model
A teacher model plus a full training run
Bits per weight, same parameter count
Usually no retraining — recalibrates existing weights
Number of weights or neurons removed
Original model plus fine-tuning to recover lost accuracy

slides.title: Worked Example: Distilling a Reasoning Model
slides.body: DeepSeek's R1 reasoning model generated long chain-of-thought traces that were then used as training data for much smaller Qwen and Llama-sized checkpoints.
bullets: The small checkpoints were fine-tuned directly on R1's reasoning traces — response-based distillation, not a from-scratch RL run
Those distilled small models outperformed same-sized models trained without access to R1's traces on math and coding evaluations
None of the small checkpoints matched full R1's own capability — distillation transfers a lot, but not everything

slides.title: Where Distillation Breaks Down
slides.body: A student is bounded by its teacher and by what its own smaller capacity can absorb.
bullets: The student's ceiling sits below the teacher's — it inherits the teacher's blind spots and biases along with its strengths
Generating high-quality teacher outputs for training data isn't free — it costs real inference time on the large model
Distilling from a closed commercial API you don't own can violate that provider's terms of service — several major labs explicitly prohibit training competing models on their outputs

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Distillation trains a small student on a large teacher's full output distribution, not just its final labels
Soft labels carry 'dark knowledge' — relative confidence across wrong answers — that hard labels discard
Response-based distillation on reasoning traces is the dominant pattern behind today's small-but-capable models
The student never fully catches the teacher, and using a closed model's outputs as training data can carry real ToS risk

questions.prompt: What does a student model learn from in classic knowledge distillation, beyond just the correct answer?
options: The teacher's training data, verbatim
The teacher's full (temperature-softened) output distribution across all possible answers
The teacher's raw model weights
Nothing extra — distillation only uses hard labels
questions.explanation: Softening the teacher's logits with a temperature before the softmax spreads probability across near-miss answers. Training the student to match that full distribution — not just the top answer — transfers 'dark knowledge' hard labels alone discard.

questions.prompt: Which distillation approach is most common in today's small reasoning-capable LLMs?
options: Feature-based, matching intermediate hidden states
Relation-based, matching example-to-example relationships
Response-based, fine-tuning on the teacher's generated text or reasoning traces
None — modern small models are always trained from scratch
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning a smaller model directly on a larger model's generated outputs or chain-of-thought traces — response-based distillation — is the dominant approach behind today's capable small models, as seen with DeepSeek-R1's traces distilled into smaller Qwen/Llama checkpoints.

questions.prompt: What's a real practical risk of distillation that goes beyond model quality?
options: Distilled models always run slower than the teacher
Distillation requires no data at all, which can trigger licensing issues
Training on a closed commercial API's outputs as your data source can violate that provider's terms of service
Distilled models can never be quantized afterward
questions.explanation: Several major model providers explicitly prohibit using their API outputs to train a competing model. Generating your distillation dataset from a closed provider you don't have rights to train from carries real contractual risk, separate from the technique's quality tradeoffs.

references.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network (Hinton, Vinyals, Dean — arXiv:1503.02531)

posts.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber: Patching Vulnerabilities With AI
posts.subtitle: Google's cybersecurity model finds and fixes bugs autonomously — and beats larger frontier models doing it.
posts.summary: Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, a specialized variant that autonomously finds and patches software vulnerabilities. On CyberGym it scores 86.2% versus 77.5% for its predecessor, and Google's own Chrome Security team measured 2.6x more correct patches than larger commercial models. Access is deliberately gated through a new Fairwind Program for vetted governments and critical-infrastructure operators.

slides.title: A Model Built to Find Bugs Before Attackers Do
bullets: Released September 1-2, 2026 alongside the general-purpose Gemini 3.8 Flash
Cyber variant purpose-built for autonomous vulnerability discovery and patching
Distributed only through Google's new Fairwind Program, not a public API

slides.title: The Defender's Speed Problem
slides.body: Attackers increasingly use AI to find exploitable bugs faster than human security teams can patch them, and critical infrastructure often lacks the staff to keep up.
bullets: Manual vulnerability triage doesn't scale across millions of lines of legacy code
Energy, healthcare, and financial infrastructure are named as priority targets for the program
A model that finds AND correctly patches bugs shifts the time-to-fix advantage back to defenders

slides.title: What Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber Actually Does
slides.body: It's a specialized version of Gemini 3.8 Flash trained to autonomously scan codebases, reproduce a vulnerability, and generate a working patch — not just flag a CVE pattern.
bullets: Built on the same 1M-token-context Flash backbone as the general release
Trained and evaluated specifically on vulnerability discovery and patch-generation workflows
Access gated to vetted security researchers, governments, and critical-infrastructure operators via Fairwind

slides.title: How It Stacks Up
bullets: On CWE-Bench it's essentially tied with a much larger frontier model — while costing less to run
The 2.6x Chrome-patch figure came from Google's own Chrome Security team, not a marketing benchmark

rows: leading frontier model: 47.8%, at higher cost

slides.title: A Worked Scenario: Patching a Chrome Bug
slides.body: In Google's internal Chrome Security evaluation, engineers pointed the model at real, unresolved vulnerabilities in the Chrome codebase.
bullets: Step 1: locate the vulnerable code path from a bug report
Step 2: reproduce the exploit to confirm the bug is real
Step 3: generate a patch that compiles and doesn't break existing tests
Result: correct, working patches 2.6x more often than larger commercial models attempting the same task

slides.title: Why You Can't Just Download This One
slides.body: Unlike most model launches, Cyber isn't shipping as a public API — and that's deliberate.
bullets: Fairwind Program vets applicants: governments, critical-infra operators, named software maintainers
Google's stated reasoning: an autonomous vulnerability-finder is also a ready-made offensive tool if it leaks broadly
Public benchmarks don't cover false-positive rates or patches that pass tests but miss edge cases — treat '2.6x' as directional, not a production guarantee

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber chains find, reproduce, and patch into one autonomous loop, not just CVE flagging
It already beats notably larger frontier models on CWE-Bench patch quality, at lower cost
Access is deliberately restricted via Fairwind — this is infrastructure-defense tooling, not a chatbot feature
Expect autonomous vulnerability-discovery agents to become standard tooling for defenders, and eventually attackers

questions.prompt: What does Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber do differently from a typical vulnerability scanner?
options: It only flags CVE patterns, like a scanner
It autonomously locates, reproduces, and patches vulnerabilities end-to-end
It replaces human security teams entirely
It only works on Python codebases
questions.explanation: The model chains discovery, exploit reproduction, and patch generation into one loop — most scanners stop at flagging a pattern.

questions.prompt: How is Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber distributed?
options: Public API available to any developer
Open-weights release on Hugging Face
Gated access via Google's Fairwind Program for vetted security teams
Bundled into Chrome for all users
questions.explanation: Google restricts access through the Fairwind Program to vetted governments, critical-infrastructure operators, and researchers, reflecting the dual-use risk of an autonomous vulnerability-finder.

questions.prompt: On CWE-Bench patching, how did Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber compare to a larger frontier model?
options: It scored far lower
It scored nearly identically (47.2% vs 47.8%) at lower cost
It scored twice as high
It wasn't evaluated on CWE-Bench
questions.explanation: 47.2% vs 47.8% pass@1 is essentially a tie in quality, but Google positions Cyber as the cheaper option for that performance.

posts.title: LightNav-0: Robot Navigation From a Vision-Language Model
posts.subtitle: One VLM backbone, zero task-specific heads, state-of-the-art navigation across ten simulators.
posts.summary: LightNav-0 elicits navigation directly from a pretrained vision-language model's spatial reasoning instead of training a task-specific head. Using dual-channel pointing tokens for spatial intent and a residual vector-quantized action tokenizer for embodiment-specific motion, it reaches state-of-the-art monocular success rates across all 10 public navigation benchmarks tested, with zero-shot generalization across robot types.

slides.title: Teaching a Vision-Language Model to Walk Through the World
bullets: arXiv:2608.30935, trending on Hugging Face's Daily Papers
Built on the Qwen3-VL vision-language backbone
No task-specific navigation head — the VLM's existing spatial reasoning does the work

slides.title: VLMs Already Understand Space — Nobody Was Using It
slides.body: Modern vision-language models can already point at objects, ground language in images, and reason about spatial relationships from pretraining. But most robot navigation systems still bolt a separate, task-specific prediction head onto a vision backbone and train it from scratch per task.
bullets: Task-specific heads don't transfer across robot embodiments — a drone's action space isn't a quadruped's
Retraining per task or robot is expensive and throws away the VLM's general spatial priors
The question LightNav-0 asks: can navigation be elicited directly from what the VLM already knows?

slides.title: Two Token Types Instead of a New Head
slides.body: LightNav-0 represents every navigation task through a unified token interface instead of a bespoke architecture.
bullets: Dual-channel pointing tokens express task-, scene-, and embodiment-agnostic spatial intent using the VLM's native pointing/grounding ability
A residual vector-quantized (RVQ) action tokenizer maps that spatial intent to precise, embodiment-specific trajectories
Because both are just token sequences, the same backbone generalizes across robots without retraining a head per platform

slides.title: Why This Generalizes
slides.body: Separating 'where do I want to be' (pointing) from 'how do I get my body there' (action tokenizer) is the core trick.
bullets: The pointing layer is embodiment-agnostic — identical whether the robot is wheeled or legged
The action tokenizer is the only embodiment-specific piece, and it's small relative to the VLM backbone
This split lets one model reuse a general-purpose VLM's spatial reasoning instead of learning it from scratch per robot

slides.title: Evaluation Breadth
slides.body: Rather than one narrow benchmark, the authors evaluate across the full spread of public navigation testbeds.
bullets: LightNav-ER (the embodied-reasoning checkpoint used to initialize LightNav-0) tops the complete-set average across 8 embodied-reasoning benchmarks
LightNav-0 itself reaches state-of-the-art monocular success rates across all 10 public navigation simulation settings tested
Real-world tests include zero-shot transfer across different robot embodiments and both static and dynamic targets, not just simulation

slides.title: A Concrete Handoff
slides.body: Picture a wheeled robot given the instruction 'go to the chair near the window' from a single monocular camera feed.
bullets: The VLM's pointing tokens ground 'chair near the window' to a location in the current frame, using spatial grounding learned from general pretraining, not navigation-specific data
The RVQ action tokenizer converts that pointed location into a sequence of wheel-appropriate motion tokens
Swap the wheeled base for a legged robot and only the action tokenizer's output changes — the pointing step is untouched

slides.title: Tradeoffs and Open Questions
slides.body: Leaning on a pretrained VLM's priors is powerful, but it inherits the VLM's blind spots.
bullets: Monocular-only evaluation means depth and occlusion errors from a single camera propagate straight into navigation mistakes
Performance is bounded by how good the underlying VLM's spatial grounding already is — a weaker backbone would likely undercut the whole approach
Dynamic-target navigation (moving obstacles or goals) is evaluated but is inherently the harder, less mature case versus static targets

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: LightNav-0 shows a general-purpose VLM's pretrained spatial reasoning can be redirected into navigation with just two token interfaces, no bespoke nav head
The embodiment-agnostic pointing / embodiment-specific action split is the reusable idea, even outside navigation
It's a data point for a broader trend: eliciting capabilities already latent in a big pretrained model beats training a narrow model from scratch

questions.prompt: What does LightNav-0 use instead of a task-specific navigation head?
options: A separate CNN trained per robot
Dual-channel pointing tokens plus a residual vector-quantized action tokenizer
A hand-coded path-planning algorithm
A larger VLM with more parameters
questions.explanation: It reuses the VLM's own pointing and grounding ability for spatial intent, then a compact action tokenizer converts that intent into robot-specific motion — no new head required.

questions.prompt: Why is separating 'pointing' from the 'action tokenizer' useful for generalization?
options: It makes the model faster to train from scratch
Pointing is embodiment-agnostic, so only the small action tokenizer needs to change across robots
It removes the need for any vision input
It only works for wheeled robots
questions.explanation: Where to go is the same question regardless of robot body; how to get there is embodiment-specific — splitting them lets one backbone serve many robots.

questions.prompt: What's a key limitation noted for LightNav-0's approach?
options: It requires expensive LiDAR sensors
Its navigation quality is bounded by the underlying VLM's spatial-reasoning ability, and it's evaluated monocular-only
It cannot run in real time
It only works in simulation, never on real robots
questions.explanation: Because the approach elicits capability from the pretrained VLM rather than learning spatial reasoning from scratch, a weaker backbone or single-camera blind spots directly limit performance.

references.title: LightNav-0: Eliciting VLM Spatial Intelligence for Generalist Embodied Navigation (arXiv:2608.30935)

posts.title: GRPO: Training Reasoning Models Without a Critic
posts.subtitle: DeepSeek's RL trick that scores answers against each other instead of training a second network to grade them.
posts.summary: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) drops PPO's learned critic model and instead scores each sampled response against the average of a group of responses to the same prompt. That halves the models needed in memory during training and underpins the reasoning gains behind DeepSeek-R1, but it trades that savings for higher per-prompt sampling cost and a dependency on cheap, reliable reward signals.

slides.title: The RL Algorithm Behind DeepSeek's Reasoning Gains
bullets: Introduced in DeepSeekMath (2024), scaled up in DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025)
Short for Group Relative Policy Optimization
The headline trick: drop the critic network entirely

slides.title: PPO's Expensive Extra Model
slides.body: Standard RLHF uses PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization), which needs a separate critic/value model roughly the same size as the policy model just to estimate how good a partial answer is.
bullets: That's 2 full-size models in memory (policy + critic) on top of the reference model used for the KL penalty — 3 total
The critic itself has to be trained and can be inaccurate, especially early in training
For long chains of thought, estimating per-token value is genuinely hard — a bad critic misdirects the whole update

slides.title: Score the Group Instead of a Single Answer
slides.body: GRPO samples a group of responses to the same prompt, scores each with a reward function, then computes each response's advantage as its reward normalized against the group's mean and standard deviation — no learned value model needed.
bullets: For a single prompt, sample many completions (e.g. 8-64), not just one
Advantage = (reward - group mean) / group std — this replaces what PPO's critic used to estimate
A KL penalty against a frozen reference policy still keeps the model from drifting too far, same role it plays in PPO

slides.title: GRPO vs PPO vs DPO
bullets: GRPO keeps PPO's ability to use a scalar reward function, useful when you have a verifier (e.g. does this math answer check out), rather than needing pre-collected preference pairs like DPO

slides.title: A Worked Example: Grading a Math Answer
slides.body: Prompt: 'What is the derivative of x^3 + 2x?' Sample 8 completions from the current policy.
bullets: A rule-based verifier checks each completion's final answer against the correct one (3x^2 + 2) — reward is 1 if correct, 0 if wrong
Say 5 of 8 completions are correct: group mean reward is 0.625
A correct completion gets a positive advantage (better than the group average), an incorrect one gets negative — responses are pushed apart based on outcome, not a critic's guess

slides.title: Why Verifiable Rewards Matter Here
slides.body: GRPO's normalized-group approach works best when the reward signal is cheap and reliable to compute for many samples per prompt.
bullets: Math, code (does it compile and pass tests), and structured tasks have cheap verifiers — ideal for GRPO
Open-ended tasks like creative writing don't have a clean verifier, so the reward itself becomes the weak link, not the RL algorithm
This is part of why GRPO became associated specifically with 'reasoning' models — verifiable-reward domains are where it shines

slides.title: Pitfalls and When Not to Reach for It
slides.body: GRPO isn't a free lunch — the group-sampling requirement changes the cost profile of training.
bullets: Sampling a group of 8-64 completions per prompt multiplies inference cost during training compared to PPO's single rollout, even without a critic
If every completion in a group gets the same reward (all correct or all wrong), the normalized advantage collapses toward zero and that batch teaches the model almost nothing
Needs a trustworthy reward or verifier function — a noisy or gameable reward gets amplified across the whole group, not smoothed out by a learned critic

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: GRPO replaces PPO's learned critic with a statistical baseline computed from a group of sampled responses to the same prompt
That cuts training memory roughly in half (no critic model), at the cost of needing multiple samples per prompt
It pairs best with domains that have cheap, reliable reward verification — math and code, not open-ended generation
It's the RL engine behind DeepSeek-R1-style reasoning gains, not a replacement for SFT or DPO in general alignment

questions.prompt: What does GRPO eliminate compared to standard PPO?
options: The reward function
The learned critic/value model
The KL penalty against a reference model
The policy model itself
questions.explanation: GRPO replaces the learned critic with a baseline computed directly from a group of sampled responses (the group mean reward), cutting the model count needed during training.

questions.prompt: How does GRPO compute a response's advantage?
options: A separate neural network predicts it
By normalizing that response's reward against the mean and standard deviation of a group of responses to the same prompt
By comparing to a fixed historical average across all training
Randomly, then correcting with backprop
questions.explanation: Advantage = (reward - group mean) / group std, computed fresh from each sampled group — no persistent value model required.

questions.prompt: When does GRPO work poorly?
options: When the reward or verifier is cheap and reliable, like checking a math answer
When every response in a sampled group gets the same reward, so the normalized advantage collapses toward zero
When training on code generation
When using a KL penalty against a reference policy
questions.explanation: If a group is all-correct or all-wrong, there's no relative signal left to learn from — that batch contributes almost nothing to the update.

references.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

posts.title: Claude Fable 5.1: 75% Cheaper Cache Reads, Same Base Price
posts.subtitle: Anthropic didn't raise prices — it attacked the line item that actually dominates agentic bills
posts.summary: Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.1 on September 1, 2026, cutting cache-read pricing 75% while holding base input/output prices flat, alongside real gains on agentic benchmarks like Terminal-Bench. The launch also introduced Claude Mythos 5.1, the same model under a more permissive safeguard profile for vetted users.

slides.title: Same $10 / $50 per Million Tokens. Cache Reads Just Got 4x Cheaper.
slides.body: On September 1, 2026, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1, its flagship coding and knowledge-work model, alongside a same-model sibling, Claude Mythos 5.1, for vetted trusted access.

slides.title: Agentic Coding Bills Are Won or Lost on Cache Reads, Not Output
slides.body: A coding agent re-sends the same huge context — file trees, tool schemas, prior turns — on nearly every step. Once that context is cached, you pay a discounted cache-read rate on it dozens of times per session, so that line item, not the fresh output tokens, ends up dominating the invoice.
bullets: Before 5.1: cache reads cost $1.00 per million tokens
Base input stayed $10/M and output $50/M the whole time
Long agent loops can touch a cached context 20-50+ times per task

slides.title: The Fix: Cut Cache Reads 75%, Leave Everything Else Alone
slides.body: Fable 5.1 drops cache-read pricing from $1.00 to $0.25 per million tokens — a straight 75% cut — while base input ($10/M) and output ($50/M) are unchanged from Fable 5. Anthropic frames this as an agentic-workload discount rather than a general price cut.
bullets: Input: $10/M unchanged. Output: $50/M unchanged
Anthropic's own estimate: ~25% cheaper on typical workloads, ~45% on highly agentic ones

slides.title: Fable 5 -> 5.1: The Benchmark Delta Is Real, Not Just PR
slides.body: The jump is largest on agentic, tool-using evaluations rather than static Q&A benchmarks — consistent with a model tuned for long coding/agent sessions.

slides.title: Fable and Mythos Are the Same Weights, Different Guardrails
slides.body: Mythos 5.1 isn't a separate model trained from scratch — it's Fable 5.1 running under a more permissive safeguard profile, gated to vetted trusted-access customers only.
bullets: Fable 5.1: declines or redirects requests touching cyberattacks or dangerous biology
Mythos 5.1: more permissive safeguards, restricted to vetted users
Same 1M-token context window and 128K max output on both

slides.title: Worked Example: A 40-Step Refactor Agent
slides.body: Say an agent loads a 300K-token repo context once, then re-reads that cached context on 40 subsequent tool-call turns while writing ~2K fresh output tokens per turn.
bullets: Cache reads: 300K x 40 = 12M tokens. Old cost: 12M x $1.00/M = $12.00. New cost: 12M x $0.25/M = $3.00
Fresh output: 40 x 2K = 80K tokens x $50/M = $4.00 either way
Total session cost drops from ~$16.00 to ~$7.00 — the savings come almost entirely from the cache line, which is exactly the line agentic loops rack up

slides.title: Where the Discount Doesn't Help
slides.body: The 75% cut is specific to cache reads, so it barely moves the needle for workloads that don't reuse context.
bullets: One-shot prompts with no repeated context see ~0% savings — there's nothing to cache-read
128K max output and a June 2026 knowledge cutoff are unchanged limits, not fixed by this release
Savings scale with how many times you re-read the same cached block, not with raw token volume

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Fable 5.1 (Sept 1, 2026): cache reads cut 75% ($1.00 -> $0.25/M), base pricing unchanged
Real benchmark gains on agentic tasks: Terminal-Bench 4.0 jumped from 42.0% to 55.8%
Mythos 5.1 = same model, more permissive safeguards, vetted access only
Biggest winners: long-running coding/tool-use agents that re-read a cached context many times per session

questions.prompt: What specifically changed in Claude Fable 5.1's pricing?
options: Base input and output prices were both cut 25%
Cache-read pricing dropped 75% ($1.00 to $0.25/M); base input/output stayed the same
All pricing was cut in half across the board
Output pricing increased to fund a lower input price
questions.explanation: Only the cache-read rate moved, from $1.00/M to $0.25/M. Base input ($10/M) and output ($50/M) were left exactly where they were on Fable 5 — the discount targets agentic, context-reuse-heavy workloads specifically.

questions.prompt: Why do agentic coding sessions benefit disproportionately from a cache-read discount?
options: Agents generate far more output tokens than normal chats
Agents typically re-send and re-read the same large context across many tool-call turns, so cache reads dominate their token spend
Agents don't use caching at all, so any caching feature helps them most
Agentic workloads use a different, larger context window
questions.explanation: An agent loop re-reads a cached context (repo state, tool schemas, history) on nearly every step, so cache-read tokens pile up far faster than fresh output tokens — making a cache-read discount worth far more to agents than to one-shot chat users.

questions.prompt: How do Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 differ?
options: Mythos 5.1 is a smaller, faster distilled version of Fable 5.1
They are the same underlying model with different safeguard/safety configurations; Mythos is restricted to vetted trusted-access users
Mythos 5.1 has a larger context window than Fable 5.1
Fable 5.1 is for coding, Mythos 5.1 is a separate model for creative writing
questions.explanation: Anthropic released them as the same model with different guardrail levels: Fable 5.1 declines requests touching things like cyberattacks or dangerous biology, while Mythos 5.1 runs more permissive safeguards but is gated to vetted users only.
