posts.title: Grouped-Query Attention: Shrinking the KV Cache Without Losing Heads
posts.subtitle: The middle ground between full multi-head attention and the too-lossy multi-query shortcut
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) splits the difference between multi-head attention's quality and multi-query attention's tiny memory footprint by letting clusters of query heads share a single key/value head. It's why models like Llama 2 70B can serve long contexts at a fraction of the KV-cache memory a full multi-head design would need.

slides.title: The KV Cache Is Usually the Real Memory Bottleneck, Not the Weights
slides.body: At inference time, every attention head keeps its own growing key/value cache per token generated. More heads and longer contexts mean that cache — not the model weights — is often what runs a GPU out of memory first.

slides.title: Multi-Head Attention Pays for Every Head, Every Token
slides.body: In standard multi-head attention (MHA), each of the H heads has its own K and V projection, so the cache grows with the full head count.
bullets: KV cache size per token = 2 (K and V) x num_layers x num_heads x head_dim x bytes
For a 70B-class model with 80 layers, 64 heads, head_dim 128, fp16: that's ~2.5 MB per token in cache
At long context and large batch size, this cache can dwarf the weights themselves in GPU memory

slides.title: GQA: Group Query Heads, Share Their Key/Value Heads
slides.body: GQA keeps all H query heads but splits them into G groups (G < H), where every query head in a group reads from one shared K/V head. Multi-query attention (MQA) is the extreme case, G=1: every query head shares a single K/V head.
bullets: MHA: G = H (one K/V head per query head) — best quality, largest cache
GQA: 1 < G < H (query heads share K/V within a group) — the tunable middle ground
MQA: G = 1 (all query heads share one K/V head) — smallest cache, largest quality hit

slides.title: Same 64 Query Heads, Very Different KV Cache
slides.body: Cache size scales directly with the number of KV heads (G), not the number of query heads — so GQA-8 gets most of MQA's memory win with much less quality loss.

slides.title: You Don't Have to Train From Scratch to Get GQA
slides.body: The GQA paper (Ainslie et al., 2023) showed existing MHA checkpoints can be converted via 'uptraining': mean-pool each group's key/value projections into one shared head, then continue training for a small slice of the original pretraining budget — roughly 5% in the paper's experiments — to recover most of the lost quality.
bullets: Start from a trained MHA checkpoint, not random init
Mean-pool K/V weights within each group to initialize the shared head
A short uptraining run recovers quality close to full MHA at a fraction of GQA-from-scratch cost

slides.title: Worked Example: Serving at 4K Context, Batch of 32
slides.body: Take the 70B-class shape from earlier (80 layers, head_dim 128, fp16) at a 4,096-token context and a batch of 32 concurrent sequences.
bullets: Hypothetical full MHA (64 KV heads): ~2.5 MB/token x 4,096 x 32 ≈ 327 GB of KV cache
GQA-8 (8 KV heads): ~0.31 MB/token x 4,096 x 32 ≈ 41 GB of KV cache — an 8x drop
That 8x is exactly num_heads / num_kv_heads (64/8) — the memory savings, not just a rough estimate

slides.title: When Not to Reach for GQA
slides.body: GQA trades a small amount of quality for memory and throughput — that trade isn't always worth making.
bullets: Small models (a few hundred million to low single-digit billions of params) rarely have a KV-cache-bound serving problem — MHA's simplicity may not be worth giving up
Too few KV groups (pushing toward MQA) can visibly hurt quality on tasks needing fine-grained per-head specialization
GQA reduces cache size, not compute — it doesn't by itself fix a compute-bound (not memory-bound) inference workload

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: KV cache size scales with the number of KV heads, not query heads — that's the lever GQA pulls
GQA sits between MHA (best quality, biggest cache) and MQA (smallest cache, biggest quality hit)
Llama 2 70B popularized GQA-8: 64 query heads sharing just 8 KV heads
Existing MHA checkpoints can be 'uptrained' into GQA for a small fraction of full pretraining cost

questions.prompt: In Grouped-Query Attention, what determines the size of the KV cache?
options: The number of query heads (H)
The number of KV head groups (G)
The total number of transformer layers only
The vocabulary size of the tokenizer
questions.explanation: Every query head still exists in GQA, but query heads within a group share one K/V head, so the cache — which stores K and V, not queries — scales with G, the number of groups, not H, the number of query heads.

questions.prompt: What is multi-query attention (MQA) in relation to GQA?
options: A completely unrelated attention mechanism
The special case of GQA where G equals the number of query heads
The special case of GQA where G = 1, so all query heads share a single K/V head
A version of GQA used only during training, never at inference
questions.explanation: MQA is GQA taken to its extreme: one shared K/V head for every query head (G=1). It gives the smallest possible KV cache but the largest quality hit compared to full multi-head attention.

questions.prompt: Why might a small language model skip GQA even though it works well for 70B-scale models?
options: GQA only works with fp16, not fp32
Small models rarely hit a KV-cache memory bottleneck during serving, so the quality/memory trade isn't worth making
GQA requires more transformer layers than small models have
GQA cannot be implemented for models under 1B parameters
questions.explanation: GQA exists to solve a memory problem: KV cache growing too large at long context or high batch size. Small models often aren't memory-bound in the first place, so adopting GQA there mostly just adds a quality cost with little practical benefit.

references.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (Ainslie et al., 2023)

posts.title: Prompt Caching: Reusing the KV-Cache You Already Paid For
posts.subtitle: Same prefix, same tokens — a fraction of the compute, but only if it matches exactly
posts.summary: Prompt caching lets an LLM API skip recomputing the attention keys and values for a prompt prefix it has already processed, cutting both latency and cost on repeated context. It only pays off when a prefix is reused verbatim, often enough, and within a short time window — get any of those wrong and you pay a write premium for nothing.

slides.title: The Same 30,000 Tokens, Sent Again and Again
slides.body: Every chat turn re-sends the system prompt, the tool schemas, the codebase context — and by default the model reprocesses all of it from scratch, every single time.

slides.title: Attention Scales With Input Length — Even the Part That Never Changes
slides.body: Computing the keys and values for a transformer's attention layers costs compute proportional to input length. If 95% of a prompt is byte-for-byte identical to the last request, the model still redoes that work — full price, full latency, for tokens it has already seen.
bullets: A 20K-token system prompt plus tool schema gets recomputed on every single turn
Time-to-first-token grows with prefix length, even when the prefix never changes
Cost scales with total input tokens, not with what's actually new in the request

slides.title: Cache the KV Tensors, Not Just the Text
slides.body: Prompt caching stores the computed key/value tensors for a prompt prefix in fast memory after the first request. A later request with an identical prefix skips the forward pass for those tokens entirely and only computes attention for the new suffix.
bullets: The cache key is the exact token sequence up to a declared breakpoint — not a semantic or fuzzy match
A single differing token anywhere before the breakpoint invalidates the cache for everything after it
Cached entries expire after a short TTL (commonly just minutes) if nothing reuses them

slides.title: Where You Put the Breakpoint Decides What Gets Reused
slides.body: Providers let a request mark one or more cache breakpoints — typically right after the system prompt, after tool definitions, or after a long shared document. Everything before the last breakpoint is a candidate for reuse; everything after it is computed fresh.
bullets: Static content (system prompt, tool defs, RAG documents) belongs before the breakpoint
Volatile content (the user's latest turn) belongs after it
Reordering a prompt so static content comes first is often the only change needed to make caching pay off

slides.title: Cache Reads Are Cheap; Cache Writes Are a Small Bet
bullets: Exact multipliers vary by provider, but the shape is consistent across all of them
Break-even is typically just two or three reuses of the same prefix within the TTL window

slides.title: A Coding Agent That Resends 30K Tokens of Context Every Turn
slides.body: An agent's system prompt plus the current repo's file tree and open files totals 30K tokens. The user asks five follow-up questions in a row. Without caching, all five requests reprocess the full 30K-token prefix. With a breakpoint placed right after that context, the first request pays a small write premium; the next four barely pay for the prefix at all.
bullets: Turn 1: ~30K tokens computed in full, cache written
Turns 2-5: the 30K-token prefix is read from cache almost for free — only the new turn is computed fresh
Net effect: latency and cost on turns 2-5 track the size of the new message, not the size of the accumulated context

slides.title: When Prompt Caching Doesn't Help — or Backfires
bullets: A prefix that changes on every call (e.g., a timestamp interpolated into the system prompt) never hits the cache — it just adds a write cost for nothing
Low-traffic prompts that go several minutes between calls expire before the next request arrives, so the write premium is a pure loss
Caching only covers tokens before the breakpoint — putting the volatile part first defeats the whole mechanism
It's a short-TTL cache, not a persistent store — don't design a product around it surviving hours or serving across accounts

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Put everything static and shared first, the volatile turn last, and mark the breakpoint between them
Prompt caching saves the most on long, repeated prefixes hit multiple times within the TTL — think agent loops and multi-turn chats, not one-off calls
It's an infrastructure optimization, not a correctness feature: the output is identical either way, just cheaper and faster on repeat hits
Check your provider's actual write/read multipliers and TTL before assuming it pays off — they vary and change over time

questions.prompt: What determines whether a request gets a prompt-cache hit?
options: The semantic similarity of the new prompt to a previous one
An exact match of the token sequence up to the declared cache breakpoint
Whether the same user ID sent the request
The total length of the conversation so far
questions.explanation: Prompt caching matches on the literal token sequence, not meaning — that's what makes it a different mechanism from semantic caching, which matches on similarity of an entire query.

questions.prompt: Why does placing static content (system prompt, tools) before the volatile part of a prompt matter for caching?
options: It doesn't — the model reads the whole prompt anyway
Everything after the cache breakpoint is recomputed fresh, so only content before it can benefit from caching
Static content must legally come first per API convention
It reduces the model's context window usage
questions.explanation: Only the prefix up to the breakpoint is cached; putting the part that changes every turn before that breakpoint means nothing ever gets reused.

questions.prompt: A prompt is called once every 20 minutes with an identical 10K-token prefix, and the provider's cache TTL is 5 minutes. What happens?
options: Every call is a cache write that never becomes a cache read — the TTL always expires first, so caching adds cost without ever paying it back
The cache extends its own TTL automatically whenever there's any traffic on the account
The 10K-token prefix is cached permanently after the first call
Caching still saves money because cost only depends on prefix length, not on timing
questions.explanation: If requests arrive less often than the TTL, the cache entry always expires before it can be reused — you pay the write premium on every call and never collect a cheap read.

posts.title: Continuous Batching: How LLM Servers Stop Wasting the GPU
posts.subtitle: Scheduling at the token level, not the request level, is what actually keeps GPUs fed
posts.summary: Static batching wastes GPU capacity because a batch can't start its next round until its slowest sequence finishes. Continuous (iteration-level) batching reschedules the batch after every single decoding step, so finished requests are swapped out and new ones swapped in immediately — the technique behind the throughput jump in serving engines like vLLM and Orca-style schedulers.

slides.title: A GPU running an LLM server is often idle — even under heavy load
slides.body: Batch several requests together and the batch is only as fast as its slowest member. If one sequence needs 300 tokens and its batchmates need 20, those 20-token slots sit empty for the rest of the round, burning GPU time on nothing.
bullets: Naive batching groups requests once, then runs the whole batch to completion
Real traffic has wildly different output lengths — chat replies vs. long completions
The fix: reschedule the batch after every token, not after every request

slides.title: Static batching ties every request to the slowest one in its group
slides.body: In request-level (static) batching, the server picks N requests, runs the whole forward pass loop until every one of them emits an end token, and only then admits new work. The batch's wall-clock time is set by whichever sequence generates the most tokens.
bullets: A batch of 20-token and 300-token requests takes as long as the 300-token one
Finished sequences still occupy a batch 'slot' doing nothing until the round ends
Under bursty traffic, new requests queue behind a batch that's mostly idle capacity

slides.title: Continuous batching reschedules after every decoding step
slides.body: Also called iteration-level or in-flight batching. Instead of committing to a fixed batch until it fully finishes, the scheduler runs one forward pass (one new token for every active sequence), then immediately evicts anything that just hit its stop token and splices in queued requests to fill the freed slots — every single step.
bullets: Scheduling granularity drops from 'whole request' to 'one token step'
A finished sequence's slot is reused on the very next iteration, not the next batch
Requires per-sequence KV cache state that can be attached/detached independently

slides.title: It needs flexible KV cache management to actually work
slides.body: Splicing a new request into a running batch mid-flight means the server must allocate KV cache for it on the fly and free the departing sequence's cache immediately — which is why continuous batching is almost always paired with block-based KV cache allocators like PagedAttention rather than one contiguous buffer per batch slot.
bullets: Scheduler runs once per forward pass, not once per request lifecycle
KV cache is allocated/freed per sequence, in small blocks, not per fixed batch slot
Long prompts (prefill) are often chunked so they don't stall in-flight decodes

slides.title: Worked example: three requests, one queue
slides.body: Requests A (20 tokens), B (200 tokens), and C (300 tokens) start together in a batch of size 3, and D is waiting in the queue.
bullets: Static batching: A and B finish at steps 20 and 200 but their slots sit empty; D waits until step 300
Continuous batching: the instant A finishes at step 20, D is spliced into A's freed slot and starts generating
By step 200, B's slot is freed and the next queued request starts immediately — the GPU never drops back to running fewer than 3 sequences
Net effect: total tokens generated per second of GPU time goes up because idle slots are eliminated, not because any single request got faster

slides.title: Static vs. continuous batching

rows: Waits for the current batch to fully drain
Can join on the very next step

slides.title: What it doesn't fix
slides.body: Continuous batching removes decode-time idling, but it isn't a free lunch — it shifts the bottleneck elsewhere and introduces new scheduling questions.
bullets: Prefill (processing a new prompt) is compute-bound, not slot-bound — a big prompt spliced in naively can stall every other sequence's next token, which is why chunked prefill exists
Without a fairness policy, a stream of short new requests can keep getting priority over one long-running sequence, starving it
You're still capped by total VRAM for KV cache — continuous batching fills slots faster, but can't admit a request there's no memory for
It optimizes throughput (tokens/sec across all users), not the latency of any one individual request

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Static batching wastes GPU time because a batch can't start its next round until its slowest member finishes
Continuous (iteration-level) batching reschedules after every single decode step, swapping finished sequences out and queued ones in immediately
It needs per-sequence KV cache that can be allocated and freed independently — usually paired with a block-based allocator like PagedAttention
It raises aggregate throughput, not individual request speed, and still needs chunked prefill and fairness policies to behave well under mixed workloads

questions.prompt: Why does static (request-level) batching waste GPU capacity?
options: It uses too much memory per request
The whole batch runs until its slowest sequence finishes, leaving other slots idle in the meantime
It can only process one request at a time
It doesn't use a KV cache at all
questions.explanation: A static batch is scheduled once and runs to completion as a unit. Sequences that finish early still hold a batch slot that does no useful work until the whole batch — bounded by its longest sequence — finally ends.

questions.prompt: What has to be true about KV cache management for continuous batching to work?
options: KV cache must be a single fixed-size buffer shared by the whole batch
KV cache isn't needed since tokens are generated one at a time anyway
Each sequence's KV cache must be allocatable and freeable independently, since sequences enter and leave the batch every step
KV cache must be recomputed from scratch on every decode step
questions.explanation: Because sequences can join or leave on any given step, the server needs to attach and release per-sequence KV cache on the fly — which is why continuous batching is typically paired with block-based allocators like PagedAttention instead of one fixed buffer per slot.

questions.prompt: What is a real limitation continuous batching does NOT solve on its own?
options: It can't reduce time-to-first-token for any request
It doesn't reduce GPU idle time at all
A large new prompt's compute-bound prefill can still stall other in-flight sequences unless prefill is chunked
It requires every request to have the same output length
questions.explanation: Continuous batching fixes idle decode slots, but prefill is a different, compute-bound phase — splicing in a big prompt naively can hog a whole forward pass and delay everyone else's next token, which is why serving engines add chunked prefill on top.

posts.title: OpenAI's Ten Proofs: Math You Can Verify Yourself
posts.subtitle: Ten decades-old open problems, each shipped as a Lean 4 certificate anyone can compile
posts.summary: OpenAI published ten proofs of previously open problems in math and theoretical computer science — not as benchmark scores, but as Lean 4 formalizations anyone can compile and check with the Lean kernel. The result is a rare AI capability claim that doesn't ask you to trust the lab, the model, or a grader.

slides.title: A model claimed 10 math breakthroughs. So you can check its work.
slides.body: OpenAI says an internal research model — previewed as Astra — produced solutions to ten open problems spanning sphere packing, group theory, circuit complexity, and more. Instead of a leaderboard number, what shipped is a public GitHub repo of machine-checkable proofs.
bullets: Ten problems, each unsolved for years in its field
Published as github.com/openai/ten-proofs under Apache-2.0
The claim isn't 'trust our eval' — it's 'run the checker yourself'

slides.title: Most AI capability claims can't be checked, only believed
slides.body: Benchmark scores are graded by a rubric, a human, or another LLM — all of which can be gamed, mis-specified, or simply wrong. Math is different: a proof is either logically valid or it isn't, and that's a property a computer can check mechanically.
bullets: LLM benchmarks are graded by fallible graders, not absolute truth
A stated 'SOTA score' still requires trusting the eval pipeline
Formal proof systems remove that trust requirement entirely

slides.title: Ten Lean 4 modules, one for each result
slides.body: Each of the ten results ships as its own Lean 4 file — NonSoficGroup.lean, ConnesRigidity.lean, SpherePacking.lean, Permanent.lean, and six more — built against the mathlib library with the Lake build system, alongside a research write-up and a separate document walking through the model's reasoning.
bullets: 10 named modules, each a self-contained formal proof
Built on Lean 4 + mathlib — the same toolchain professional formalizers use
A companion 'reasoning walkthroughs' document explains the approach in prose
Anyone can clone the repo and run Lake to verify every proof compiles

slides.title: Worked example: sphere packing bounds
slides.body: One of the ten, formalized in SpherePacking.lean, tightens the known asymptotic bounds on how densely spheres can pack high-dimensional space — a decades-old problem in discrete geometry with implications for coding theory.
bullets: The Lean file encodes the improved bound as a formal theorem statement
Lean's kernel checks every inference step against that statement, not English prose
If the file compiles with zero unproven gaps, the bound is verified — full stop
The hard part was never checking the logic; it's finding a proof strategy that works

slides.title: Two ways to trust a capability claim

rows: Only by re-running the same eval
A wrong theorem statement, correctly proved

slides.title: What a green checkmark doesn't prove
slides.body: Lean verifies that the proof is logically valid for the statement as written. It says nothing about whether that statement is the theorem anyone actually cares about — a common way formalization efforts go wrong.
bullets: A perfectly valid proof of a subtly mis-stated theorem is worthless
Formalizing the right statement is still a human (or model) judgment call
Ten wins say nothing about a general success rate — this isn't a benchmark pass rate
This is evidence of a capability, not proof the model can do unsupervised research

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: OpenAI published 10 solutions to open math/TCS problems as Lean 4 proofs, not benchmark scores
Formal verification means the claim can be checked by a proof kernel, not just believed
The repo (github.com/openai/ten-proofs) is public, Apache-2.0, and runnable by anyone
Verified logic still depends on formalizing the right statement — that step stays a judgment call

questions.prompt: What makes this claim different from a typical LLM benchmark score?
options: It was graded by a panel of human mathematicians
The proofs are formalized in Lean 4, so a proof kernel — not a grader — checks validity
It used a larger test set than usual
OpenAI published the model's raw weights alongside it
questions.explanation: Benchmark scores depend on trusting the eval and grader. Here, each result is a Lean 4 proof that anyone can compile — the Lean kernel mechanically checks validity, removing the need to trust the lab's grading.

questions.prompt: Even with a Lean file that compiles cleanly, what risk remains?
options: The proof might use too much GPU memory
Lean proofs can't be checked offline
The formalized theorem statement itself might not match the real-world claim being made
Mathlib doesn't support advanced number theory
questions.explanation: Lean guarantees the proof is logically valid for the statement as written — it can't tell you whether that statement correctly captures the theorem you actually care about. Mis-stating the theorem while proving it perfectly is a known failure mode in formalization work.

questions.prompt: Where and under what license are the ten proofs published?
options: A private OpenAI research portal, license unspecified
github.com/openai/ten-proofs, under Apache-2.0
Only as a PDF, with no runnable code
Behind the ChatGPT API as a paid tool
questions.explanation: The formal proofs, built on Lean 4 and mathlib, are published in a public GitHub repository under an Apache-2.0 license — anyone can clone it and run the Lake build to verify the results themselves.

references.title: openai/ten-proofs — Lean 4 formalizations on GitHub

posts.title: Hy4 Preview: Tencent's 770B Open-Weight MoE Flagship
posts.subtitle: Apache-2.0 weights, a 1M-token window, and DeepSeek-style sparse attention
posts.summary: Tencent's Hunyuan team open-sourced Hy4 preview, a 770B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (49B active per token) with a 1M-token context window, released under Apache-2.0. It pairs DeepSeek-style sparse attention with a multi-token-prediction head, and ships with Tencent's own internal expert evaluations against GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3.

slides.title: Tencent open-sources a 770B flagship, not a distilled sample
slides.body: Hy4 preview lands with full Apache-2.0 weights: 770B total parameters, 49B active per token, and a context window rated past 1M tokens. Most models at this scale stay behind an API.
bullets: 770B total / 49B active parameters (MoE)
1M-token context window
Apache-2.0 — weights, not just an API

slides.title: Frontier scale and open weights rarely ship together
slides.body: The biggest MoE models are usually either fully closed behind an API, or open-sourced at a fraction of frontier scale. A 770B-parameter release under a permissive license, with a working 1M-token window, is unusual on both axes at once.
bullets: Serving a model this large still requires multi-GPU infrastructure, even 'open'
1M-token context multiplies KV-cache memory pressure at inference time
Tencent ships it anyway — self-hosted, ModelScope, GitCode, and Hugging Face

slides.title: 78 layers, 256 routed experts, sparse attention throughout
slides.body: The backbone is 78 layers: the first is a dense feed-forward block, the remaining 77 replace it with MoE — 256 routed experts plus 1 always-on shared expert, with the top 8 routed experts activated per token.
bullets: Attention: Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention (Gated DSA) with IndexCache for cross-layer index reuse
iHC (identity Hyper-Connections) improves information flow between layers
Hidden size 6144, 64 attention heads, 120,832-token vocabulary
A multi-token-prediction (MTP) head adds 10B params (0.7B active) purely for speculative decoding

slides.title: What 'sparse' means for a single forward pass
slides.body: Of the 770B total parameters, only 49B are active for any given token — about 6.4% of the model. Attention doesn't scan the full context densely either: Gated DSA uses the IndexCache to select which past tokens matter before spending compute on them.
bullets: 49B / 770B ≈ 6.4% of parameters active per token
The MTP head predicts extra tokens ahead, letting the base model verify several at once
Net effect: frontier-scale capacity, inference cost closer to a much smaller dense model

slides.title: Tencent's own internal expert evaluation
Read the internal eval for what it is
slides.body: The numbers above come from 163 internal experts rating outputs on 203 engineering tasks — Tencent's own methodology, not an independent third-party benchmark. That doesn't make them meaningless, but it does set the bar for how much weight to put on them.
bullets: 163 raters, 203 tasks, average score plus win/tie/loss split — a real, if self-run, eval
Tencent itself labels this release 'an early version' with room left in pre- and post-training
Independent benchmarks (public leaderboards, third-party evals) haven't landed yet at time of writing
Open weights mean the community can run its own comparisons directly

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Hy4 preview: 770B total / 49B active MoE, 1M-token context, Apache-2.0 weights
Sparse attention (Gated DSA + IndexCache) and an MTP head both target inference cost, not just quality
Tencent's internal eval shows narrow wins over GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 — self-reported, not third-party
It's explicitly a preview: Tencent says pre- and post-training both still have headroom

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of Hy4 preview's parameters are active for any given token?
options: About 6.4%
About 25%
About 50%
100% — it's a dense model
questions.explanation: 49B of the 770B total parameters are active per token (49/770 ≈ 6.4%), since only the top-8 routed experts plus the shared expert fire for each token — the rest of the 256 routed experts sit idle.

questions.prompt: What should you keep in mind about the GLM 5.3 / Kimi K3 comparison numbers in the release?
options: They come from a public, third-party leaderboard
They're from Tencent's own internal panel of 163 experts rating 203 tasks — not an independent benchmark
They were generated automatically by another LLM grader
They only cover coding tasks
questions.explanation: The win/tie/loss and average scores are Tencent's own internal evaluation methodology. That's a real, structured eval, but it isn't the same evidentiary bar as an independent third-party benchmark run by someone outside the company.

questions.prompt: What is the multi-token-prediction (MTP) head in Hy4 preview for?
options: Translating between languages
Increasing the model's total parameter count for benchmarks
Predicting several tokens ahead to support speculative decoding and speed up generation
Compressing the KV cache to save memory
questions.explanation: The MTP head (10B added params, 0.7B active) predicts extra tokens ahead of the main generation, which the base model can then verify in parallel — a form of self-speculative decoding that reduces the number of full forward passes needed per output token.

posts.title: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: Skipping Most of the Context
posts.subtitle: A cheap indexer picks the few thousand tokens actually worth attending to
posts.summary: Full attention costs grow quadratically with context length, so at 100K+ tokens most of that compute scores tokens the model will barely use. Sparse attention schemes like DeepSeek's fix this with a cheap 'lightning indexer' that picks a small, relevant subset of past tokens before the expensive attention math ever runs.

slides.title: Attention gets quadratically more expensive, not linearly
slides.body: Standard self-attention compares every token to every other token. Double the context length and you roughly quadruple the attention compute — the single biggest cost driver once contexts pass 100K tokens.
bullets: Full attention cost scales as O(L²) in sequence length L
At long context, attention — not the feed-forward layers — dominates latency and cost
Most of those pairwise comparisons contribute almost nothing to the output

slides.title: Long context makes the waste obvious
slides.body: For any given query token, only a handful of past tokens are actually relevant to predicting the next word — a citation, a variable definition, a earlier turn in the conversation. Full attention still scores every single one.
bullets: A 128K-token document might have only a few thousand tokens relevant to any one query
Dense attention pays full price to discover that most tokens don't matter
Naive fixes (fixed sliding windows, strided patterns) throw away tokens by position, not relevance

slides.title: A lightning indexer scores relevance before attention runs
slides.body: DeepSeek Sparse Attention adds a small, cheap side-network — the 'lightning indexer' — that assigns each past token a lightweight relevance score against the current query. Only the top-scoring tokens are kept for the real, expensive attention computation.
bullets: The indexer is deliberately lightweight — its own cost is a small fraction of full attention
Every past token gets scored, but only the top-k highest-scoring ones proceed to real attention
Real attention then runs over that small selected set, not the full context
Effective cost drops from O(L²) toward O(L·k), where k is fixed regardless of context length

slides.title: Trained by distillation, not bolted on after the fact
slides.body: A sparse selector trained from scratch tends to silently drop tokens the model actually needed. DeepSeek's approach instead warm-starts from a model that still uses dense attention, then trains the sparse student to match what the dense teacher would have attended to.
bullets: Start from a checkpoint trained with ordinary dense attention
Train the indexer + sparse attention path to approximate the dense model's attention pattern
This keeps quality close to dense attention instead of degrading once tokens get dropped
The indexer effectively learns 'which tokens would dense attention have cared about?'

slides.title: Worked example: a long document query
slides.body: Picture a 128K-token codebase pasted into context, and a query token asking about a function's behavior partway through generation.
bullets: The indexer cheaply scores all prior tokens against that query — the function's own definition, its call sites, and nearby comments score high
Unrelated boilerplate elsewhere in the file scores low and gets skipped
Real attention then runs only over that small relevant subset — a fraction of the full 128K tokens
The output should look close to what full dense attention over all 128K tokens would have produced

slides.title: Three attention strategies at long context

rows: Top-k tokens chosen by learned relevance
Depends on indexer quality; mitigated by distillation

slides.title: Where this doesn't pay off
slides.body: Sparse attention isn't free — the indexer itself adds a pass over the whole sequence, and a poorly trained one can miss tokens the model genuinely needed, with failures that are easy to miss in normal evals.
bullets: Below a certain context length, the indexer's overhead isn't worth the savings
An undertrained indexer creates a silent recall problem: dropped tokens the model needed but never got to see
Distillation quality against the dense teacher is what determines whether sparsity is safe to ship
It optimizes inference and long-context training cost — it doesn't reduce total parameter count

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Full attention's O(L²) cost makes long context expensive — most token comparisons don't matter
A cheap lightning indexer scores every past token, then keeps only the top-k for real attention
Training the sparse path to imitate a dense-attention teacher (distillation) is what preserves quality
Below a length threshold, or with an undertrained indexer, sparsity isn't worth the tradeoff

questions.prompt: Why does full self-attention become the dominant cost at long context lengths?
options: Because feed-forward layers scale worse than attention
Because attention cost scales quadratically (O(L²)) with sequence length, while other layers scale roughly linearly
Because the tokenizer becomes slower on long inputs
Because KV cache memory doesn't affect compute cost
questions.explanation: Self-attention compares every token to every other token, so its cost grows as O(L²) in sequence length L. Feed-forward layers scale closer to linearly, so past a certain length, attention dominates total compute and latency.

questions.prompt: What does the 'lightning indexer' do in DeepSeek Sparse Attention?
options: It compresses the model's weights to reduce memory
It cheaply scores every past token's relevance to the current query, so only the top-k proceed to full attention
It replaces the tokenizer with a faster one
It reorders tokens by position before training
questions.explanation: The indexer is a lightweight side-network that assigns a relevance score to every past token for the current query. Only the highest-scoring top-k tokens go on to the expensive real attention computation, cutting effective cost from O(L²) toward O(L·k).

questions.prompt: Why is the sparse attention path typically trained by distilling from a dense-attention model, rather than trained from scratch?
options: Distillation is required by the Lean proof checker
It makes the model smaller in total parameter count
Training from scratch is impossible with mixture-of-experts layers
It teaches the indexer to approximate what a dense model would have attended to, avoiding silently dropped tokens that hurt quality
questions.explanation: An indexer trained from scratch risks silently dropping tokens the model actually needs, degrading quality in ways that are hard to catch. Warm-starting from a dense-attention checkpoint and distilling against it keeps the sparse selection close to what full attention would have chosen.

posts.title: Attention Sinks: Why the First Few Tokens Hold a Cache Together
posts.subtitle: A streaming LLM trick that keeps perplexity from collapsing at any length
posts.summary: Sliding-window KV caches keep memory bounded but collapse in quality the moment the very first tokens get evicted. Keeping a handful of those initial tokens permanently in the cache — as 'attention sinks' — fixes this with almost no extra cost, letting a model serve an effectively unbounded conversation.

slides.title: Why can't a chatbot just run forever?
slides.body: Every transformer keeps a growing key/value cache for every token it has seen. Left alone, that cache eventually eats all your memory — so serving systems cap it. The naive fix for capping it quietly breaks the model.
bullets: KV cache grows with every generated token
Production serving needs a hard memory ceiling
The obvious fix — a sliding window — has a hidden failure mode

slides.title: Sliding windows collapse the moment token 0 leaves
slides.body: The intuitive fix is to only keep the most recent N tokens in the KV cache and drop the rest, like a ring buffer. It works right up until the buffer wraps around and evicts the very first tokens of the sequence — at which point output quality falls apart.
bullets: Drop oldest tokens once the cache hits its size limit
Fine as long as eviction hasn't reached the start of the sequence
The instant token 0 is evicted, perplexity spikes and generation degrades

slides.title: Softmax has nowhere to put 'no attention'
slides.body: Attention scores for every query must sum to 1 across whatever keys are visible. If a token has nothing useful to attend to, the softmax still has to spend its probability mass somewhere — and models learn to dump that leftover mass onto the first few tokens, regardless of their content.
bullets: Softmax output always sums to 1 — there's no 'attend to nothing' option
Early tokens absorb huge attention scores unrelated to their meaning
Researchers call this an attention sink: a release valve baked in by training
Evicting the sink tokens removes that valve, and scores redistribute badly

slides.title: Cache the sinks, slide the rest
slides.body: The fix keeps the KV cache split into two parts: a small fixed set of sink tokens from the very start of the sequence that are never evicted, plus a normal sliding window of the most recent tokens. Everything in between is dropped.
bullets: Reserve a few slots (often just 4) for the first tokens — never evict them
Slide the remaining budget over the most recent tokens as normal
No retraining or architecture change needed on many existing models
Position indices are reassigned within the cache, not tied to original sequence position

slides.title: A support bot running for 100,000 turns on a 2,048-token budget
slides.body: Imagine a chat agent with a hard 2,048-token KV cache, deployed for a support session that runs to 100,000 tokens over the day.
bullets: Plain sliding window: stable until token 2,049 pushes out token 0-3, then quality visibly degrades for the rest of the session
Sink + window: tokens 0-3 stay pinned as sinks; tokens 2,044 onward slide normally; quality stays flat all day
The sink tokens don't need to be semantically special — even the BOS token works
Memory footprint is identical to the plain sliding window — the fix is where you evict from, not how much you keep

slides.title: Three ways to bound a KV cache
What this trick does not give you
slides.body: Attention sinks buy stability, not memory. It's easy to mistake a stable streaming session for a model that 'remembers' the whole conversation.
bullets: Content from the evicted middle is genuinely gone — the model can't recall it
This is a stability fix, not a substitute for real long-context or retrieval
Too few sink tokens (e.g. just 1) can still be unstable; the right count is model-dependent
For tasks that truly need old context back, pair this with RAG or a summarization step, not sinks alone

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Sliding-window KV caches cap memory but collapse when they evict the first tokens
Early tokens absorb disproportionate attention because softmax must sum to 1 — an 'attention sink'
Pinning a handful of sink tokens while sliding the rest restores stability at near-zero extra cost
It fixes generation quality for infinite streams — it does not restore lost mid-conversation memory

questions.prompt: Why does a plain sliding-window KV cache degrade once it evicts the first few tokens?
options: Those tokens contain the model's system prompt
Softmax attention must sum to 1, and models learn to dump excess attention onto early tokens as a release valve
The tokenizer reassigns different IDs after eviction
GPU memory becomes fragmented at that point
questions.explanation: Because softmax scores must sum to 1 across visible keys, models learn to route leftover attention mass to a few fixed early tokens regardless of content. Remove those tokens and the model has nowhere well-calibrated to put that mass, so outputs degrade.

questions.prompt: What's the key structural change attention sinks make to a sliding-window cache?
options: It doubles the cache size to hold more recent tokens
It retrains the model with a new loss function
It permanently reserves a few slots for the earliest tokens while the rest of the cache slides normally
It compresses old tokens into a single summary vector
questions.explanation: The cache is split into a small fixed pool of never-evicted sink tokens plus a normal sliding window for recent tokens — no compression or retraining required.

questions.prompt: What can attention sinks NOT do?
options: Keep perplexity stable across very long streams
Work on existing models without fine-tuning
Restore information from tokens that were evicted from the middle of the conversation
Bound the KV cache to a fixed memory footprint
questions.explanation: Attention sinks fix generation stability, not memory — content evicted from the middle of the stream is genuinely gone. Recovering it requires retrieval or summarization, not sink tokens.

posts.title: BDH-CQ: A 150M Model Breaks the ARC-AGI Cost Frontier
posts.subtitle: Recurrent latent reasoning beats verbalized chain-of-thought on cost per solved task.
posts.summary: Pathway's BDH-CQ solves ARC-AGI-1 puzzles by updating a fixed-size recurrent memory and iterating in latent space instead of writing out chain-of-thought text. At 150M parameters it hits 29.5% pass@2 for about $0.0007 per task, landing beyond the previously reported cost-accuracy frontier for the benchmark.

slides.title: A 150M-Parameter Model Just Broke a Cost Frontier
slides.body: Pathway's BDH-CQ reasons inside a recurrent latent state instead of writing out its thinking — and it's dramatically cheaper per solved ARC-AGI-1 task than anything reported before it.

slides.title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Gets Expensive Fast
bullets: Most reasoning models solve hard puzzles by verbalizing step-by-step thought — every extra token of reasoning is extra compute you pay for at inference time.
ARC-AGI-1 tests abstract visual pattern induction from a handful of examples; frontier LLMs have needed heavy scaling (bigger models, longer traces) to make real progress on it.
That leaves a cost-accuracy frontier: plot accuracy against $/task and most systems that get more accurate also get proportionally more expensive.

slides.title: Think in a Recurrent Memory, Not in Text
bullets: BDH-CQ is built on Dragon Hatchling (BDH), Pathway's post-transformer recurrent architecture where neuron-like units communicate through low-rank interactions.
Instead of a growing KV cache, it keeps a fixed-size recurrent associative state that gets updated as each in-context demonstration is read.
At query time it doesn't emit an intermediate chain-of-thought — it solves the task through iterative computation inside that latent state, then produces the answer directly.

slides.title: An 'Effort' Knob That Adds Latent Iterations, Not Tokens
bullets: The model exposes LOW vs. HIGH effort settings — more effort means more rounds of internal latent iteration on the same fixed-size memory, not longer written output.
Moving from LOW to HIGH effort raised pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 from 21% to 29.5%.
Because the extra computation stays in latent space rather than generated tokens, the cost curve for more 'thinking' is far flatter than it is for verbalized chain-of-thought.

slides.title: What More Effort Buys You

rows: More latent iterations; ~0.85 H200-GPU-seconds and ~$0.0007 per task

slides.title: Solving a Grid-Transformation Puzzle
slides.body: An ARC-AGI task shows a handful of input/output grid pairs that share a hidden transformation rule, then asks the model to apply that rule to a new input grid.
bullets: BDH-CQ reads each demonstration grid and folds it into its recurrent associative state — no text description of the rule is ever generated.
At the new query grid, it runs its latent iterations to converge on an answer grid directly from that compressed state.

A standard LLM attempting the same task would typically verbalize a hypothesis about the rule in text first ('the shape rotates 90° and recolors...'), burning output tokens whether or not that hypothesis is right.

slides.title: Where This Approach Runs Into Limits
bullets: No verbalized reasoning trace makes it harder to inspect why the model reached a given answer — there's no chain-of-thought to audit.
The result is demonstrated on ARC-AGI-1, not the harder ARC-AGI-2 successor or general open-domain reasoning — it's a specialist result, not a general-purpose reasoning replacement.
Training leans on a curated mixture of ARC-style data (RE-ARC, ConceptARC, ARC-Heavy and similar augmentations) — the efficiency gain is tied to a task family with that kind of structure.
At 150M parameters it isn't a general chat or knowledge model; it trades broad capability for narrow, cheap iterative reasoning.

slides.title: The Big Idea
bullets: Reasoning cost doesn't have to scale with output tokens — BDH-CQ moves the 'thinking' into a fixed-size recurrent latent state instead of generated text.
An effort knob that adds latent iterations (not tokens) gives a cheaper way to trade compute for accuracy than longer chain-of-thought.
It's a data point for a broader post-transformer direction (Dragon Hatchling) where memory and inference share the same computational fabric rather than being bolted together.

questions.prompt: What does BDH-CQ do instead of writing a verbalized chain-of-thought to solve an ARC-AGI-1 task?
options: It iterates inside a fixed-size recurrent latent state and outputs the answer directly
It samples multiple text completions and votes on the majority answer
It retrieves the answer from a lookup table of past ARC solutions
It fine-tunes its weights on each new puzzle before answering
questions.explanation: BDH-CQ folds each demonstration into a recurrent associative memory and solves the query through iterative latent computation — never generating an intermediate text reasoning trace.

questions.prompt: Going from LOW to HIGH effort in BDH-CQ mainly changes what?
options: The number of output tokens it generates
The number of latent iteration rounds on its fixed-size memory
The number of model parameters that get activated
The size of the training dataset used
questions.explanation: Effort in BDH-CQ controls how many rounds of internal latent iteration the model runs on its recurrent state — not how much text it writes, which is why the cost curve stays flat compared to verbalized reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why is BDH-CQ's result described as breaking a 'cost-accuracy frontier' rather than just a new accuracy record?
options: It's the first system to ever solve any ARC-AGI-1 task
It reaches its accuracy at a lower reported cost per task than any prior plotted system at that accuracy or better
It has more parameters than any competing model
It was the first model trained without any ARC-style data
questions.explanation: A cost-accuracy frontier plots the best accuracy achieved at each price point; BDH-CQ's 29.5% pass@2 at roughly $0.0007/task lands beyond every previously reported point on that frontier, not just above one specific model's accuracy.

posts.title: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813: Preview Graduates to Flagship
posts.subtitle: Selectable reasoning effort, a bolted-on speculative decoder, and native support for OpenAI's Responses API.
posts.summary: DeepSeek shipped V4-Pro-0813, the official production release superseding the V4-Pro preview: three selectable reasoning-effort levels replace the old fixed thinking budget, a new DSpark speculative decoding module speeds up generation, and the model now natively supports OpenAI's Responses API — all on the same 1M-token, unchanged-parameter base.

slides.title: DeepSeek's Flagship Leaves Preview
slides.body: After roughly four months in preview, DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 is the official production release — same base model, several production-focused upgrades bolted on.

slides.title: A Preview Tag Doesn't Survive Contact With Production
bullets: DeepSeek-V4-Pro had been running as a preview build for months while frontier competitors kept shipping — a preview label makes teams hesitant to build production agents on top of it.
The preview shipped with a single fixed thinking budget, which is a blunt instrument: the same reasoning depth for a one-line autocomplete and a multi-file refactor.
Agentic and tool-calling workloads exposed rough edges that only show up under real production traffic, not static benchmarks.

slides.title: What 0813 Actually Changes
bullets: Replaces the single fixed thinking budget with three selectable reasoning-effort levels — low, high, and max — so callers pick depth per request.
Adds a DSpark speculative decoding module attached to the existing V4-Pro-preview model structure, aimed at faster token generation without changing the base weights.
Adds native support for OpenAI's Responses API, easing integration for teams already building against that interface.
Model name, parameter count, and the 1-million-token context window are unchanged from the preview.

slides.title: Speculative Decoding, Bolted On Rather Than Retrained
bullets: Speculative decoding works by having a cheap draft step propose several tokens ahead, which the full model then verifies in parallel — accepted tokens are 'free', rejected ones fall back to normal generation.
DSpark is attached to the same V4-Pro-preview weights rather than requiring a retrained base model, which is why the released parameter count and context window didn't move.
This mirrors a broader industry pattern: ship a speculative-decoding layer as an add-on to cut latency/cost on an already-trained model instead of re-training for speed.

slides.title: Preview vs. 0813

rows: Adds native OpenAI Responses API support

slides.title: Picking Effort Per Request
slides.body: A team running a coding agent harness can now route work by task shape instead of paying one fixed reasoning cost for everything.
bullets: Quick autocomplete-style edits get routed at 'low' effort — fast, cheap, good enough for a single-file change.
A gnarly multi-file refactor or a failing-test debugging loop gets routed at 'max' effort, trading latency and cost for deeper reasoning.

Official pricing starts at $0.435 / $0.87 per 1M input/output tokens on a cache miss, with peak/off-peak rates added a few days after launch — worth checking the current rate card before committing usage at scale.

slides.title: Read the Benchmark Fine Print
bullets: Third-party benchmark write-ups on 0813's exact SWE-bench Verified score don't fully agree with each other — treat any single quoted percentage with some skepticism until you've checked the eval harness it came from.

Independent agentic-coding leaderboards that score full open-ended agent loops (not just single-patch generation) place it further from the top than patch-style benchmarks suggest — strong at some task shapes, weaker at others.
Pricing tiers (peak/off-peak) were introduced shortly after launch, so a quoted price from launch day can already be stale.

slides.title: The Big Idea
bullets: 'Preview to GA' upgrades are often about production ergonomics (effort controls, API compatibility, latency) more than raw capability — the base model here didn't even change size.
Speculative decoding modules like DSpark are a cheap way to cut latency/cost on an already-trained model without a full retrain.
Always sanity-check third-party benchmark claims against multiple sources — coding-agent evaluations especially disagree depending on harness setup.

questions.prompt: What replaced the single fixed thinking budget in DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813?
options: A larger parameter count
Three selectable reasoning-effort levels (low, high, max)
A longer context window
A separate model for each task type
questions.explanation: 0813 lets callers pick low/high/max reasoning effort per request instead of paying one fixed thinking budget for every call.

questions.prompt: What does the DSpark module added in 0813 actually do?
options: Retrains the base model on new data
Increases the context window to 1M tokens
Speculative decoding — draft tokens proposed cheaply, verified in parallel by the full model
Adds a new vision encoder
questions.explanation: DSpark is a speculative decoding module attached to the existing preview weights: a cheap draft step proposes tokens ahead, and the full model verifies them in parallel to speed up generation without retraining.

questions.prompt: Why does the post caution against trusting a single quoted SWE-bench score for V4-Pro-0813?
options: Because DeepSeek has not published any benchmark numbers
Because independent write-ups report differing scores, and full agentic-loop leaderboards rank it differently than patch-style benchmarks
Because SWE-bench does not evaluate coding models
Because the model changes its score every day
questions.explanation: Different third-party sources quote different SWE-bench Verified numbers for the same release, and separate leaderboards that score full agent loops (not just single patches) place it differently — a reminder to check the eval setup behind any single number.

posts.title: HNSW: How Vector Search Skips Scanning Everything
posts.subtitle: A layered small-world graph trades a sliver of recall for enormous query speed.
posts.summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph-based index most vector databases use for approximate nearest-neighbor search. By stacking sparse-to-dense graph layers and greedily walking toward the query, it turns a linear scan over millions of embeddings into a handful of graph hops — at the cost of memory, exactness, and cheap deletes.

slides.title: Nobody Scans 10 Million Embeddings Per Query
slides.body: Exact nearest-neighbor search over embeddings costs O(N) per query. HNSW is the graph structure most vector databases use to get sub-linear search instead.

slides.title: Brute-Force kNN Doesn't Scale
bullets: Exact k-nearest-neighbor search compares the query vector against every stored vector — cost grows linearly with the number of embeddings.
A RAG system with 10M+ chunks and multiple queries per second can't afford a full scan per request and still feel interactive.
The fix is approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search: give up a small, tunable amount of recall in exchange for order-of-magnitude faster queries.

slides.title: Small-World Graphs, Stacked Like a Skip List
bullets: HNSW builds several graph layers stacked on top of each other; each vector is randomly assigned a top layer via an exponentially decaying probability, so higher layers have far fewer nodes.
A search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily walks toward whichever neighbor is closest to the query.
Once no neighbor at the current layer is closer, the search drops down one layer and keeps walking — narrowing in fast at the top, then refining at the bottom where the full graph lives.
It's the same idea as a skip list, but the 'sorted order' is replaced by vector similarity.

slides.title: Three Knobs, One Recall/Speed/Memory Triangle
bullets: M — the max number of neighbor edges per node per layer (commonly in the teens to tens). Higher M raises recall and memory use, and slows insertion.
efConstruction — the candidate list size used while building the graph. Higher gives a better-connected graph at slower build time.
efSearch — the candidate list size used at query time. Higher raises recall at the cost of query latency, and can be tuned per query without touching the index.

slides.title: HNSW vs. the Alternatives

rows: High — graph edges plus vectors, usually in RAM
No cheap delete; tends to need periodic rebuilds
Simpler to build, generally weaker recall than HNSW

slides.title: Walking a Query Through a 10M-Vector Index
slides.body: A RAG system has embedded 10 million document chunks at 768 dimensions and built an HNSW index with M=32, efConstruction=200.
bullets: A user's query embedding arrives. Search enters at the top layer, which might hold only a few hundred nodes.
It greedily hops toward the query by vector distance, drops a layer once nothing closer is available, and repeats — layer by layer, down to layer 0 where every vector lives.
At the bottom layer it expands a candidate list of size efSearch (say, 100) and returns the top-10 nearest chunks — typically in single-digit milliseconds instead of scanning all 10 million vectors.

slides.title: Where HNSW Bites You in Production
bullets: Memory-hungry: the graph edges plus the full vectors normally need to sit in RAM for speed, so 10M x 768-dim floats already cost multiple gigabytes before graph overhead.
No cheap delete: removing a node breaks its neighbors' edges, so most implementations tombstone deleted vectors and periodically rebuild rather than delete in place.
Recall is probabilistic, not guaranteed: the greedy walk can get stuck in a local optimum and miss a true nearest neighbor, especially rare edge cases.
Aggressive metadata filtering that shrinks the candidate pool too much can tank recall — filtering interacts badly with a graph built for the unfiltered space.

slides.title: The Big Idea
bullets: HNSW replaces a linear scan with a layered graph walk — sparse layers narrow the search fast, dense layers refine it.
Three knobs (M, efConstruction, efSearch) let you trade recall, speed, and memory against each other — and efSearch is tunable per query.
It's the default ANN index in most vector databases today, but IVF and hybrid indexes still matter when memory or update-heavy workloads make HNSW's tradeoffs a bad fit.

questions.prompt: Why do vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search instead of exact kNN at scale?
options: Exact kNN is illegal to use in production systems
Exact kNN's cost grows linearly with the number of vectors, which is too slow for large, interactive workloads
ANN always returns more accurate results than exact search
Exact kNN can only be run on GPUs
questions.explanation: Brute-force kNN compares the query against every stored vector — O(N) per query. ANN methods like HNSW trade a small amount of recall for far faster, sub-linear queries.

questions.prompt: In HNSW, what happens as a search moves from the top graph layer toward the bottom?
options: The search restarts from scratch at each layer with no memory of progress
It greedily narrows in using sparse, long-range connections first, then refines with the denser bottom layer
It switches to a brute-force scan at the bottom layer
Layers are used only during index construction, not during search
questions.explanation: Top layers are sparse, so the walk covers large distances fast; the search drops a layer whenever it can't get closer, ending at the dense bottom layer for fine-grained refinement — similar to how a skip list narrows in on sorted data.

questions.prompt: Which HNSW parameter can be changed per query, without rebuilding the index, to trade latency for recall?
options: M
efConstruction
efSearch
Vector dimensionality
questions.explanation: efSearch controls the candidate list size used at query time and can be raised or lowered per query. M and efConstruction are baked into the graph at build time and require reindexing to change.
